title: ‘The Voice of Hind Rajab’ Director Calls Israeli Investigation Into Killing of Palestinian Girl a ‘Smokescreen’: ‘What Is Needed Is Justice’
full_text: Aug 21, 2026 2:40am PT ‘The Voice of Hind Rajab’ Director Calls Israeli Investigation Into Killing of Palestinian Girl a ‘Smokescreen’: ‘What Is Needed Is Justice’ By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest Jacob Elordi Ducks James Bond Question at London World Premiere of Ridley Scott’s ‘The Dog Stars’ When Asked if He’s Been Auditioning: ‘I’m Here on Holiday’ 56 minutes ago Watermelon Pictures Acquires Diego Luna’s Migration Drama ‘Ashes’ (EXCLUSIVE) 19 hours ago Christine Vachon on Why Landing Pedro Pascal to Replace Joaquin Phoenix in ‘De Noche’ Gave Todd Haynes the ‘Happy Ending’ He Deserved 22 hours ago See All Willa Kaouther Ben Hania , the director of last year’s Oscar-nominated docudrama “ The Voice of Hind Rajab ” — about the killing of a 5-year-old Palestinian girl in Gaza by Israeli forces — has rejected the news that Israel is launching an investigation into Rajab’s death, describing it as “a smokescreen.” On Wednesday, the Israeli military admitted that its troops had opened fire on the car carrying Rajab and six members of her family in January 2024. Rajab later died following a three-hour call with the Palestinian Red Cross in which she pleaded for help. An ambulance sent to rescue her was also attacked by the Israeli military, killing two medics. Related Stories 'The Odyssey' Photo Books Reveal Behind-the-Scenes Secrets of Filming the Trojan Horse, Battles and More Korea Box Office: 'The Odyssey' Bests 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' The Israeli Defense Forces repeatedly claimed that its troops had not been in the area at the time of the killings. But investigations by media outlets found evidence that nearby Israeli tanks were responsible, with the death of Rajab becoming one of the most high-profile incidents in the early months of the war in Gaza, prompting outrage around the world. Popular on Variety “Following review of the findings and due to alleged failures in the coordination of the movement of the Palestine Red Crescent ambulance, it has been decided to initiate a criminal investigation of the incident by military police criminal investigation division,” the Israeli military said on Wednesday, more than two years after the killing. In a statement on her Instagram page, Ben Hania — who used the recording of Rajab’s call to the Red Cross in her film, which would go on to win numerous honors including the grand jury prize in Venice and nominations from both the BAFTAs and Oscars — pushed back against the investigation. “This announcement is a smokescreen. For more than two years, the evidence has been there: independent investigations, satellite imagery, ballistic analysis. And there was the most devastating evidence of all: Hind’s own voice, describing the Israeli tanks circling around her. What more did we need?” she wrote. “Did we really have to wait for the accused to decide to investigate itself (yes, itself!) before these facts could finally be taken seriously?” Ben Hania added: “Meanwhile, the Israeli military continues to kill Palestinians in Gaza, while the occupation intensifies in the West Bank. What is needed now is not a public relations operation. title: Woody Harrelson Ready to Direct Another Live Film, Compares Jason Bateman’s ‘The Cackling of the Dodos’ to Martin McDonagh and the Coen Brothers
full_text: Aug 21, 2026 2:22am PT Woody Harrelson Ready to Direct Another Live Film, Compares Jason Bateman’s ‘The Cackling of the Dodos’ to Martin McDonagh and the Coen Brothers The actor stopped by the Variety Lounge at the Sarajevo Film Festival, where he also said he is taking baby steps into stand-up comedy By Rafa Sales Ross Plus Icon Rafa Sales Ross Guest Contributor Latest Asghar Farhadi Condemns Politicians and Media for Focus on ‘Difference’ and ‘Hate’: ‘Why Do You Think a Mother in Afghanistan Is Different Than Your Mom?’ 21 hours ago Woody Harrelson Discusses Reteaming With Matthew McConaughey on ‘Brothers’: ‘If You’re Looking for ‘True Detective,’ It’s Not This’ 3 days ago Urša Menart Recalls Finding Inspiration on Influencers’ Fake Tragic Life Stories for Intimate Dramedy ‘Everything That’s Wrong With You’ 6 days ago See All Almost a decade after taking on an unusually challenging directorial debut with the world’s first live-streamed feature film in “Lost in London,” Woody Harrelson is finally ready to direct again. The actor revealed his desire to be back behind a camera, as well as his latest creative venture as a budding stand-up comic, while at the Variety Lounge, presented by the Sarajevo Film Festival and BH Telecom. Despite having a career spanning more than 100 films, starring in major franchises such as “The Hunger Games” and “Star Wars,” leading TV hits such as “True Detective” and “Cheers,” and now hosting a podcast, Harrelson said directing “Lost in London” was “the most challenging thing I have ever experienced.” Related Stories 'This Summer Will Be Different' Netflix Series Adds 6 to Cast as Production Begins Netflix Hires Warner Bros. Exec Katie Martin Kelley as Communications VP To celebrate the 10th anniversary of his debut, Harrelson is thinking about revisiting the format, albeit in a less dramatic fashion. “I’ll go to one of the streamers and say: Hey, do you want to try doing a live film? Maybe like an hour, though, and certainly not like [‘Lost in London’], when there were 14 different locations and hundreds of extras.” “It nearly killed me,” he recalled of directing and starring in the high-pressure shoot. “I think it could be fun to try it again, but this time I think it will be easier having the benefit of having done it before and knowing 190 things I would have done differently. I can hopefully fix it, make it better.” On the subject of stressful new ventures, Harrelson has recently taken on a new practice: stand-up comedy. “I have a lot of friends who do stand up and I admire them a lot,” he said. “To me, it’s the most difficult, challenging form of entertainment because it’s you, a microphone, and the audience. And you’ve got to make them laugh. Anyway, I’ve been making notes and everything. I am sure I’m going to just absolutely crash the first time, but I think I’ll try.” Can we expect a one-hour comedy special anytime soon? “I haven’t even tried it!,” he exclaims. “No! Can’t expect the special [laughs].” We can expect some comedy, however, with Harrelson set to appear on Apple TV’s latest comedy series “Brothers.” The series reunites Harrelson with “True Detective” co-star Matthew McConaughey to play fictionalized versions of themselves. In the show, created by “The Office” producer Lee Eisenberg, their friendship is put to the test once they uncover a decades-old secret: they might actually be brothers. The story is inspired by real-life events, coming to the screen a few years after Harrelson went public with the fact that his father met McConaughey’s mother just around the time the “Dallas Buyers Club” actor was conceived. Harrelson had known McConaughey’s mother for 25 years when she pulled him to one side and told him she knew his dad. “I’m thinking, well, that’s weird that she’s never told me this. I’m thinking, well, what’s behind this story?” Has working with McConaughey in a series loosely inspired by their own lives meant learning something new about each other? “I don’t know if we learned anything new,” he said. “I mean, we’ve been hanging out a long time, and we’re very good friends. I guess I learned that he’s one of the funnest people I know. I love hanging out with him. I can barely get enough of him. And he is very much like my brother. I think the show turned out real good.” Another Harrelson project to look forward to is Jason Bateman ’s “The Cackling of the Dodos,” which marks another big reunion: with Sam Rockwell, with whom he shared the screen in “Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri.” The Netflix film is the first production under Harrelson’s new banner, Children at Play, which he launched with “Champions” producer Anna Schwartz. The producer found the script, which Harrelson said was “pretty good.” He told Schwartz he would do the film if she got Rockwell to sign on, which she did. Then, Harrelson asked for Bateman to direct. And Schwartz booked the “Ozark” star. Harrelson was particularly elated to get Bateman, whom he called “the guy with the Midas touch.” “They did a rewrite, and it really became fantastic. Much more like a Martin McDonagh or Coen Brothers type of vibe. I think that one’s going to be real good. I have a good feeling about it.” Ted Sarandos Meets Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Unveils Netflix India Storytelling Initiative Cricket Rules India’s Streaming Viewership in New Ormax StreamView Report AI-Created Indian Musical Microdrama ‘Mohini – Khud Se Pyaar’ Unveils Debut Track ‘Angaat Aalay Ka’ (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Macbeth,’ ‘Gaslit,’ ‘Silent Rebellion’ Win Raindance Awards With ‘Serena’ Winning Inaugural Best Horror Prize ‘Operation Safed Sagar’: Inside Netflix’s High-Altitude Bet on the Untold Story of the India-Pakistan Kargil War ‘The Traitors’ India Sets August Season 2 Bow on Prime Video (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments... title: Sriram Raghavan Developing New Thriller in the ‘Johnny Gaddaar’ Zone for India’s Matchbox Shots as ‘Operation Safed Sagar’ Soars on Netflix Charts (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Aug 21, 2026 2:15am PT Sriram Raghavan Developing New Thriller in the ‘Johnny Gaddaar’ Zone for India’s Matchbox Shots as ‘Operation Safed Sagar’ Soars on Netflix Charts (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Amazon MGM Studios Unveils Teaser for Kunal Kemmu’s ‘Vibe’ (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago Soccer Drama ‘Forza’ Sets Indonesia Release, Global Rollout (EXCLUSIVE) 20 hours ago Karan Johar Hails ‘Unpredictable Nature’ of ‘The Traitors’ India as Season 2 Becomes Prime Video’s No. 1 Non-English Title (EXCLUSIVE) 21 hours ago See All Matchbox Shots Indian auteur Sriram Raghavan is developing a new thriller for Matchbox Shots set in the tonal zone of his 2007 film “Johnny Gaddaar,” as the Mumbai production house grows its slate on the strength of the global Netflix success of war series “ Operation Safed Sagar .” “Johnny Gaddaar” was a twist-laden neo-noir heist thriller that marked Neil Nitin Mukesh’s screen debut alongside Dharmendra, and has since grown into a cult favorite. Related Stories Netflix Teen Thriller 'The Body’ Sets November Release Date, Drops First Look Photos (TV News Roundup) 'This Summer Will Be Different' Netflix Series Adds 6 to Cast as Production Begins “I am personally working on a couple of subjects with them,” Raghavan tells Variety . “One is a true crime sort of thing which I am sort of adapting in my own way. And the other is a fiction, it is a thriller, and I mean next year is 20 years of ‘Johnny Gaddaar,’ so something I want to do in that zone.” The director has yet to settle on a title. Popular on Variety Beyond the Raghavan projects, Matchbox’s slate includes a second season of “Scoop” for Netflix with Hansal Mehta, a still-untitled dark comedy thriller from Vasan Bala and another untitled thriller directed by Jasmeet Reen. Matchbox’s Sanjay Routray says the range is deliberate. “We want to cater to a diverse audience, both in India and internationally,” he says. “The common thread across all those titles is that each one is an untold or uniquely told story with genuine entertainment value. The genre changes, the scale changes, the format changes. The promise to the audience does not.” Meanwhile, Raghavan traces his relationship with Matchbox back to its earliest days when it was known as Matchbox Pictures. “Matchbox began, I mean as a company, with ‘ Andhadhun ,'” he says. “So we tasted success very, very early, and I am very happy that now ‘Safed Sagar’ is like doing sort of similar sort of wave, creating waves in the OTT [streaming] kind of a thing.” The 2018 blind-pianist thriller “Andhadhun” became the company’s breakout hit, grossing $62.4 million worldwide, against a production budget of INR160 million ($1.7 million), a return the company has since held up as the benchmark for the rest of its slate. Much of that total came from an unexpected market: released in China in 2019 under the title “Piano Player,” “Andhadhun” opened to $10.6 million and went on to gross $47.1 million there, more than three times its India total of $13 million, at the time making it the fifth-highest-grossing Indian film ever released in the Middle Kingdom, trailing only “Dangal,” “Secret Superstar,” “Bajrangi Bhaijaan” and “Hindi Medium.” Routray points to “Andhadhun” as his go-to example of finding commercial potential in unlikely material. “On paper, a thriller about a blind pianist sounds like a niche festival film,” he says. “On screen, ‘Andhadhun’ became a global blockbuster. The hook was always there. It was just about believing in the director and backing the story with everything we had.” Raghavan also directed the Matchbox-produced “Merry Christmas,” with Routray producing, and was involved with “Monica, O My Darling.” “It is a comfort zone for me,” Raghavan says. “I work there, Sanjay is a friend of mine, and we know each other for many, many years.” Netflix series “Operation Safed Sagar” was filmed inside active air force installations under strict operational protocols, using actual MiG fighter jets alongside cockpit simulation technology built specifically for the production. Routray says the shoot, which involved a crew of more than 450 people working at altitudes above 16,000 feet, tested the limits of what the company had built over the years. “At that height there is no existing infrastructure,” he says. “Logistics, power, accommodation, safety, medical support, all of it had to be created from scratch and then sustained for a long-haul shoot. It also proved to us, and to our partners, that Matchbox can deliver at that scale.” By its second week on the platform, the series had climbed to No. 2 on Netflix’s global chart for non-English shows, landed in the top 10 in 40 territories and stayed at No. 1 in India. It’s the second consecutive Matchbox series to reach those heights: Anubhav Sinha’s “IC 814: The Kandahar Hijack” also debuted at global No. 2 and India No. 1, a feat Matchbox says makes it the only Indian production house to place back-to-back series near the top of Netflix’s worldwide charts. The company’s push beyond Hindi-language projects produced its first Malayalam-language film, “Thrishanku,” a romantic comedy starring Arjun Ashokan and Anna Ben that Matchbox produced alongside Lacuna Pictures and Clock Tower Pictures & Co. Written and directed by Achyuth Vinayak, the film released in theaters in 2023, following a couple whose plan to elope is complicated when the man’s sister decides to elope as well. Matchbox has also been acquiring book rights, including “The Gurugram School Murder” and “The Johnson and Johnson Files,” as it builds out a pipeline of owned intellectual property, the same approach that turned the book “Flight into Fear” into “IC 814.” For Matchbox’s Patil, success today comes down to one word. “Longevity,” she says. “Stories that stay with audiences long after the release window has passed. In our experience, if a story achieves longevity, the numbers and the recognition tend to follow on their own. They are outcomes, not targets.” That philosophy extends to how the company spends. Patil says Matchbox invests in development on projects long before a greenlight or outside funding arrives, money committed with no guarantee of a return. “We know exactly how much we can afford to lose on a bet, and we never bet more than that,” she says. “That is what allows us to keep taking punts year after year.” Routray adds that the discipline cuts both ways: “For any film to land, there has to be a perfect marriage between the numbers and the creative intent. If either side of that equation is broken, we would rather walk away early than force a project into existence. Some of our best decisions have been the films we did not make.” Routray also points to a fact he thinks audiences rarely register: overall theatrical footfalls have declined even as the cost of going to the cinema has risen. “The film has to be worth leaving the house for,” he says. “That reality shapes what we greenlight and how we make it, far more than people realize.” Matchbox is also exploring animation, AI-assisted production and other emerging formats, while recommitting to theatrical releases alongside its streaming slate. The film has sold to Fandango for Italy, Palace Films for Australia and New Zealand, Vertigo Releasing for Hungary, CinemArt for the Czech Republic and Slovakia, MCF for ex-Yugoslavia and Bulgaria, Mayfly for Poland, Inoekino for the CIS, Taip Toliau for Lithuania, Estinfilm for Estonia and Riga FF for Latvia, with Warner Bros. Discovery has also bought broadcast rights for HBO Europe and streaming platform HBO Max in multiple Central and Eastern European territories after the theatrical run. Related Stories News Lav Diaz's Venice Title 'Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors' Boarded By Heretic For Sales News Heretic To Handle International Sales On 'Adult Supervision' With Gustaf Skarsgård, Fares Fares & Linus Wahlgren -- Cannes Market Adult Supervision – known locally as Arkipelag – follows three fathers who chaperone their teenage daughters on a rowdy school trip to a remote island. As tensions mount and old resentments resurface, the boundaries between authority, friendship and violence become increasingly blurred. Above is the film’s first international trailer. Watch on Deadline The film brings together three prominent Scandinavian actors: Gustaf Skarsgård ( Vikings ), Fares Fares ( The Nile Hilton Incident ) and Linus Wahlgren ( Partisan ). Schulman, one of Sweden’s best-known authors and co-host of the popular Alex & Sigge’s podcast, makes his feature directorial debut with the film, which he also wrote. The deals follow Heretic’s international launch of the film at the Cannes market. The film features cinematography by Jakob Ihre, longtime collaborator of Joachim Trier and Emmy-winning director of photography on HBO’s Chernobyl . Adult Supervision is produced by Warner Bros. International Television Production Sweden, with Christina Legkova as producer and Johan Hedman and Sofie Palage as executive producers. It is co-produced by RMV Film, Tiisch Film, Film Stockholm and Scanbox Entertainment, with support from the Swedish Film Institute and the Swedish Agency for Economic and Regional Growth. The film is bing distributed in Sweden by Scanbox Entertainment. Christina Legkova, producer at Warner Bros. International Television Production Sweden, said: “We’re thrilled to see Adult Supervision connecting with audiences and distribution partners across so many territories ahead of its world premiere. Alex has created something that is both darkly entertaining and emotionally honest, and we’re excited to share the film with international audiences beginning at Fantastic Fest.” Ioanna Stais, Head of Sales at Heretic, added: “We’re thrilled by the response to Adult Supervision and proud to have already partnered with such a strong group of leading international distributors. title: Folk Horror ‘Wolf Days,’ Family Drama ‘The First Week of August’ Win at Sarajevo Industry Awards
full_text: Aug 21, 2026 2:00am PT Folk Horror ‘Wolf Days,’ Family Drama ‘The First Week of August’ Win at Sarajevo Industry Awards By Christopher Vourlias Plus Icon Christopher Vourlias Latest ‘You Don’t Belong Here’ Director Florin Şerban Sets Next Feature After Winning Locarno’s Golden Leopard (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago ‘Mother’ Director Teona Mitevska Preps Sequel to Feminist Satirical Drama ‘God Exists, Her Name Is Petrunya’ (EXCLUSIVE) 3 days ago ‘Shame and Money’ Director on Sundance-Winning Drama About a Kosovo Family in Free Fall: ‘It’s a Look Into the Past and a Warning to the Future’ 5 days ago See All "The First Week of August" (Courtesy Sarajevo Film Festival) Emilija Gašić’s folk horror “Wolf Days” and Filip Mojzeš’ family drama “The First Week of August” won the top prizes in the Sarajevo Film Festival ’s CineLink Industry Days, the industry section focused on projects in different stages of development from Southeast Europe, the Middle East and North Africa. Gašić’s sophomore feature, which is produced by Serbia’s Non-Aligned Films and co-produced by Istok Films and Restart, won the Eurimages Co-Production Development Award, a cash prize of €20,000 ($23,000). Related Stories ‘The Odyssey’ Craze Continues as New BFI Imax Screenings Sell Out in Under 30 Minutes (EXCLUSIVE) 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day,' 'The Odyssey' Battle Atop U.K., Ireland Box Office The film follows a woman facing menopause who turns to a folk healer who draws her into a series of increasingly ridiculous rituals, driving her to the edge of madness in search of her own liberation. Gašić’s first feature, “78 Days,” premiered in the Bright Futures section of the Intl. Film Festival Rotterdam. Popular on Variety In a director’s statement provided to Variety , Gašić said: “‘Wolf Days’ is inspired by my encounters with many women who have been misdiagnosed, dismissed and misunderstood within a deeply patriarchal healthcare system. This film seeks to uncover and challenge the taboos surrounding women’s health, especially menopause, and to expose the power imbalances that define both medical and personal relationships.” The Eurimages Special Co-Production Development Award, also a cash prize of €20,000 ($23,000), went to “Mamayi,” from Ukrainian writer-director Oleksandr Roshchyn and producer Packgauz. Set in 2009, the film follows two TV reporters forced into a dirty election campaign for a pro-Russian candidate who struggle to stay honest with their work and the people. The film marks the directorial debut of Roshchyn, known as the cinematographer behind films including 2021 Berlin Crystal Bear winner “Stop-Zemlia” and 2025 Berlin Golden Bear contender “Timestamp.” “During a lengthy assignment in Ukraine, I began observing and imagining the personal drama of a journalist unfolding against the backdrop of pivotal socio-political events,” Roschchyn said in a director’s statement. “[‘Mamayi’] is a film about witnessing the approach of a catastrophe — about the ability to foresee it and the inability to prevent it.” In the Works in Progress strand, the HBO Award in the amount of €30,000 ($35,000) went to Filip Mojzeš’s “The First Week of August” (pictured), produced by Tamara Babun Zovko and Matija Drniković for Wolfgang&Dolly and Black Photon. The family drama is set during an idyllic island vacation that takes a tumultuous turn when a mother’s sudden physical outburst towards her 10-year-old son exposes hidden tensions and lingering conflicts within the family. As with his previous short films, which premiered in competition at Sarajevo, Mojzeš’ feature debut “also explores complex family dynamics,” he said in a director’s statement. “In that sense, the film represents a natural continuation of my ongoing preoccupation with the fragility of the nuclear family.” Also in Works in Progress, the Post Republic Award, offering €30,000 ($35,000) in post-production services, went to “The White Week,” directed by Bojan Vuletić and produced by Jelena Mitrović, Boris T. Matić, Lana Matić, Danijel Hočevar and Ivan Đurović for Film House Baš Čelik, Propeler Film, Vertigo and Artikulacija. The film follows an 11-year-old boy who exploits his brother’s tragic death to fight his father and his community, until his lies expose the hypocrisy and corruption beneath a seemingly moral society. The Avanpost Media Award, offering €30,000 ($35,000) in post-production services, went to Kazakh director Assel Aushakimova’s “Pay the Bill,” produced by Assel Yerzhanova for Film Film Film. It tells the story of a 65-year-old woman who receives an unexpected late-night phone call from a police officer, leading to a difficult night and day searching for her daughter that plunges her into a world of general indifference. Other prizes handed out in the CineLink Co-Production Market include the Film Center Montenegro Award, which gave a €10,000 ($11,700) cash prize to Turkish director Selcen Ergun’s “How to Disappear in the Lake.” The Kosovo Cinematography Center CineLink Award in the amount of €10,000 ($11,700) went to “The Taste of the Peach,” by Georgian filmmaker Elena Mikaberidze, who also received the Next Step Studio CineLink Award. The Artekino International Prize in the amount of €6,000 ($7,000) went to “Forbidden Fruit,” from Slovenia’s Urška Djukić Lecamus. In the CineLink Drama strand, the Croatian Audiovisual Center Drama Award in the amount of €15,000 ($17,500) went to the family drama series “You Can Always Come Back,” from creator Tena Gojić and writer Hana Jušić. The TV Drama Vision Pitch Award went to the Croatian political thriller “Stringers,” from writer-creator Nikola Kuprešanin. Lastly, the Female Voices CineLink Award, a €20,000 ($23,000) cash prize handed out in partnership with the Slovenian Film Center and the United Nations in Bosnia and Herzegovina, went to the horror-comedy series “Little Yugoslavia,” from writer-creators Teona Strugar Mitevska and Sonja Prosenc. The Sarajevo Film Festival runs Aug. 14 – 21. title: Jacob Elordi Ducks James Bond Question at London World Premiere of Ridley Scott’s ‘The Dog Stars’ When Asked if He’s Been Auditioning: ‘I’m Here on Holiday’
full_text: Aug 21, 2026 1:45am PT Jacob Elordi Ducks James Bond Question at London World Premiere of Ridley Scott’s ‘The Dog Stars’ When Asked if He’s Been Auditioning: ‘I’m Here on Holiday’ By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest Jacob Elordi Ducks James Bond Question at London World Premiere of Ridley Scott’s ‘The Dog Stars’ When Asked if He’s Been Auditioning: ‘I’m Here on Holiday’ 31 minutes ago Watermelon Pictures Acquires Diego Luna’s Migration Drama ‘Ashes’ (EXCLUSIVE) 19 hours ago Christine Vachon on Why Landing Pedro Pascal to Replace Joaquin Phoenix in ‘De Noche’ Gave Todd Haynes the ‘Happy Ending’ He Deserved 21 hours ago See All Getty Images Jacob Elordi was the star guest in London on Thursday night as he touched down for the world premiere of Ridley Scott ‘s latest feature “ The Dog Stars .” The actor’s arrival in Leicester Square was immediately soundtracked by the noise of screams from fans, including from a group of girls leaning out of nearby window, who dramatically upped both their volume and pitch when the actor turned to wave at them. The actor also sparked swoons when he walked and posed on the carpet with Rak Jasper, one of three acting dogs who appear in the movie. Related Stories 'Hunting Wives' Sets Season 2 Release Date, Drops First-Look Photos Netflix Plans Week-Long 'Beef' Free Wellness-Centered FYC Events Throughout Los Angeles (EXCLUSIVE) Alongside Elordi, “The Dog Stars'” other cast — including Josh Brolin, Margaret Qualley and Guy Pearce — were in attendance at the Odeon Luxe cinema, together with the legendary director himself (who premiered his last movie, “Gladiator 2,” in the same spot less than two years ago). Popular on Variety Speaking to Variety , Elordi described Scott as “the king of movies,” saying that working with him was “such a treat — a dream come true.” He added: “I don’t think I’ll ever have an experience like that. Yeah. He’s one of a kind and he’s a pioneer of of modern cinema.” With the casting for James Bond now very much underway and Elordi continuing to have a strong presence among the favorites for the coveted role, Variety also managed to sneak in a question about whether he’d been involved in the auditions. It was a query he, clearly with some experience now under his belt, expertly ducked. “I’m here on holiday,” he said with a smile. Photo by Jeff Spicer/Getty Images for The Walt Disney Company Limited Getty Images for The Walt Disney “The Dog Stars,” from Disney’s 20th Century Studios, is a post-apocalyptic sci-fi, directed by Scott from a screenplay by Mark L. Smith and based on Peter Heller’s 2012 novel of the same name. The film is set in the aftermath of a devastating flu pandemic that has almost eradicated humanity, and follows a former civilian pilot and hardened ex Marine as they confront outside threats and hold onto the possibility of a better life. Ironically, Scott had originally eyed his “Gladiator 2” leading man Paul Mescal for the main role, but he had to drop out due to scheduling conflicts with the Beatles’ biopics, and Elordi stepped in. Speaking to Empire Magazine before the premiere, Brolin said that he almost quit “The Dog Stars” after just one day due to Scott’s intense filmmaking process. “It bugged me out, and I got really scared,” he said, adding that he called his agent to say “I want out. Something’s really wrong and I’ve got to get the f— out of here.” However, he said things settled eventually down enough for him to continue, describing Scott’s approach as “stratospherically creative and stratospherically dangerous.” “The Dog Stars” will release in theaters on Aug. 28. title: ‘Free Nelson Mandela’ Maker Rogan Productions Opens South Africa Office & Tweaks Management Set Up
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News California Film & TV Tax Credits In Peril As Sacramento Deal Falls Apart: Exclusive Read the full story By Jesse Whittock , Jake Kanter August 21, 2026 1:35am Soleta and James Rogan Rogan Productions EXCLUSIVE: Fresh off producing Channel 4’s Free Nelson Mandela , Rogan Productions has opened an office in South Africa. The new unit, Rogan South Africa , will be a production base in Johannesburg with close links to Cape Town. This marks the first permanent international expansion for the 13-year-old London-based company. At the same time, Rogan is tweaking its management set-up with founders James and Soleta Rogan taking on co-CEO titles, as well as leading Rogan SA as they search for a local senior producer. The pair has jointly led Rogan since launch, but to this point Soleta Rogan has been Managing Director and James Rogan the Creative Director. Mark Hedgecoe is Head of Rogan Scotland in Glasgow, but is moving to STV in October, with a replacement being sought. Related Stories News David Bowie's Final Decade To Be Celebrated In Documentary Feature From Channel 4, Rogan & Dogwoof News BBC Marking Five Years Since George Floyd's Death With Feature Doc Soleta and James Rogan have close ties with South Africa and their recent three-part doc series Free Nelson Mandela was a well-reviewed look at the life of the anti-apartheid campaigner and political prisoner who became the country’s first Black president in 1992. BBC Studios is shopping it internationally. Watch on Deadline Rogan also produced Original Sin: My Son the Killer for now-defunct South African streamer Showmax. The feature doc, co-produced with fellow UK firm Electric Shadow Company in association with Brazil’s Red Earth and South Africa’s Combined Artists, follows Thea Pretorius, mother of Gerhard Jansen van Vuuren, who murdered his girlfriend Andrea Venter in front of her neighbours, security guards and CCTV cameras in 2011 and then escaped two years later just before his trial. “South Africa has always inspired and captivated us with its deep creativity and extraordinary stories so setting up a base here has been a long-held ambition for us,” said James Rogan. “Whether in drama or documentary, there are world class filmmakers in South Africa, that we are looking forward to working with, and new platforms that are showcasing the brilliance and the potential of African stories. Rogan SA connects us to a storytelling tradition that is hugely powerful and it is an exciting next step on our creative and commercial journey.” Rogan’s productions include Boom Box: Beats and Betrayal for HBO Max, Bowie: The Final Act for Film4/Channel 4, and BAFTA winners Grenfell: Uncovered for Netflix and Uprising for the BBC. “With our broader footprint, Rogan is afforded the scope to deliver more stories in more formats, to more audiences,” said Soleta Rogan. “This has been an aim we have been actively working towards for the past couple of years, with the idea first being ruminated long before that. title: ‘The Marching Band’ Review: Brothers From Opposite Worlds Are United by Music in a Finely Tuned French Crowdpleaser
full_text: Aug 21, 2026 12:55am PT ‘The Marching Band’ Review: Brothers From Opposite Worlds Are United by Music in a Finely Tuned French Crowdpleaser Belatedly opening Stateside after proving a domestic hit in 2024, Emmanuel Courcol's film succumbs to formula, but is lifted by its precise construction and strong lead performances. By Caspar Salmon Plus Icon Caspar Salmon Latest ‘PAW Patrol: The Dino Movie’ Review: The Dog-Cop Franchise Pushes an ACAB Message, Only It’s All Canines Are Benevolent 2 weeks ago See All Courtesy of Playtime “ The Marching Band ” blasts through more story in its first 12 minutes than many films now manage in two hours. In those first 720 seconds we meet Thibaut ( Benjamin Lavernhe ), a well-heeled classical music conductor in Paris, who discovers that he will need to find a blood marrow transplant as he has leukemia; he learns that his sister is not a match, as he was adopted; he then discovers a biological brother, Jimmy ( Pierre Lottin ), who was not adopted and still lives in a disadvantaged working-class community in the north of France; he asks his new-found brother to help him, and Jimmy accepts. That concision is evident in an almost brutally economical edit and in sharp, precise writing which provides narrative elements and deftly sketches character before moving busily on. Just as a marching band keeps time with its feet, so “The Marching Band” strides on, hitting the requisite notes and paying attention to the melody, sure, but especially making sure to hold the beat and keep the show on the road. This attention to rhythm helps director Emmanuel Courcol ‘s film to stay true as it navigates some rather rocky terrain, for it is at once a mismatched buddy movie, a socially conscious crowdpleaser in the vein of, say, “The Full Monty,” and a sophisticated psychological drama à la française . Related Stories Netflix Buys Wu-Tang Clan Doc 'The Disciple' Directed by Joanna Natasegara (EXCLUSIVE) Netflix Sets Its Longest Theatrical Window Ever for Oscar Hopeful 'La Bola Negra,' Moving Up Release Date That the film mostly pulls this off is testament to its formal precision and to a central pairing of actors, in Lavernhe and Lottin, who manage to find subtlety where broad strokes would seem to be called for. More than two years after its Cannes premiere, “The Marching Band” opens theatrically in the U.S. this week through Greenwich Entertainment. Once the film has dispatched its initial premise — the leukemia storyline is essentially a MacGuffin, and soon disappears for a sizable stretch — it can get down to the business of developing a bond between the characters, and establishing its (gentle) social critique. Jimmy, who works as a cook in a canteen, has a musical gift, which throws into sharp relief the different chances both men have been given in life. A scene in which this terse, withdrawn young man is revealed to have perfect pitch is typical of “The Marching Band’s” best qualities in its appealing first hour or so: Thibaut asks his brother to identify the sounds of a honking car or a barking dog, and Jimmy shyly names the correct chords. That pertness should be unbearable, but the scene is written in a minor key and performed by both actors to match, favouring eye contact and murmurs; the sheer brevity prevents it from becoming gloopy or crass. The casting of Lavernhe and Lottin is particularly inspired, as the two performers bring an affect to these characters that mimics the story’s dynamic. Lavernhe, credited as “Benjamin Lavernhe de la Comédie-Française,” comes from a background in classical theatre, and performs his role with worldly elegance; Lottin, meanwhile, is a veteran of the popular comedy franchise “Les Tuche”, centering on a working-class family from the north of France. These sensibilities come together in the film’s tight dialogue, as when the two men meet and Thibaut introduces himself: “My name is Thibaut Desormeaux, and two weeks ago I learned I have leukemia…” Jimmy: “Ah, shit.” Thibaut: “Yes.” Popular on Variety Lottin is particularly intelligent in articulating Jimmy’s shame at his lack of means and achievement, inflected with pride and a lightly worn resentment that comes out in bursts of passive-aggressive joshing; meanwhile, Lavernhe deftly portrays the well-meaning and likable Thibaut as, conversely, insufficiently ashamed of his good fortune, at least early on: This smooth Parisian bobo does not even perceive how he flaunts his wealth and education. In parallel, “The Marching Band” depicts a working-class community struggling with poverty and unemployment, for whom the musical collective — in which Jimmy plays the trombone, alongside his on-off girlfriend Sabrina (Sarah Suco) — has become a lifeline. Thibaut becomes involved, but will he be able to save the band from ruin? Here, the film closely mirrors the 1996 British comedy “Brassed Off,” making it a dead cert that we’ll eventually get a barn-burning finale showing the federating power of music in adversity. Revealing how that comes about would enter spoiler territory, but saying that it happens at all is germane, as it shows that the film finally falls victim to formula. In these pre-ordained moments — a surfeit of montages, an artificial falling-out between the brothers, the occasional dip into the saccharine — “The Marching Band” becomes a touch pleased with itself. The formula works (and the film has the domestic box-office receipts to prove it), but it detracts somewhat from the project’s smarts elsewhere. In a well-presented technical package, plaudits should go to editor Guerric Catala for a cut that attempts to shun sentiment, and to Christel Birot for costumes that smartly outline both character and class differences via the means of double denim or a freshly pressed felted overshirt. The music department, as well as Courcol’s lively directing and writing, must be commended for scenes of the brass ensemble playing and rehearsing, in a constantly dynamic interaction with dialogue. The zippy soundtrack, much like the film itself, veers between surprisingly choice cuts (the aching “I Remember Clifford” by Lee Morgan) and rabble-rousing crowdpleasers (Dalida, or the overture from “Aida”). Ravel’s “Bolero,” which repeats the same phrase over and over again but with tonal differences each time, also features. ‘The Marching Band’ Review: Brothers From Opposite Worlds Are United by Music in a Finely Tuned French Crowdpleaser Reviewed online, Aug. 19, 2026. title: ‘Good People’ Review: Milcho Manchevski’s Haunting Documentary Revisits the Kočani Nightclub Fire Through Survivors’ Eyes
full_text: Aug 21, 2026 12:07am PT ‘Good People’ Review: Milcho Manchevski’s Haunting Documentary Revisits the Kočani Nightclub Fire Through Survivors’ Eyes World premiering in competition at Sarajevo, the Golden Lion-winner’s self-funded requiem is a strikingly spare and harrowing portrait of social collapse. By Beatrice Loayza Plus Icon Beatrice Loayza Latest Diego Luna on Challenging How Migrants Are Viewed With ‘Ashes’: ‘We’re Not Thinking About What They Left Behind’ 3 days ago ‘Supporting Role’ Review: Dato Bakhtadze Captivates in a Nocturnal Odyssey Through Tbilisi 4 days ago ‘Night Nurse’ Review: Two Perverts Join Forces in a Gloriously Deviant Oddity About a Caretaker Drawn Into Her Patient’s Grifting Games 1 month ago See All Courtesy of Sarajevo Film Festival On March 16, 2025, a fire broke out at the Pulse nightclub in the small North Macedonian town of Kočani, injuring hundreds and killing 63 people due to burn damage, smoke inhalation and other physical traumas sustained while attendees scrambled to flee through the venue’s sole exit. The club had only one fire extinguisher and its ceiling was made of highly flammable material, while the venue’s 250-person capacity was exceeded by double the amount of people, most of them between the ages of 16 and 25. Related Stories Jessica Simpson Doc Set at Netflix From ‘Robbie Williams’ Director Joe Pearlman (EXCLUSIVE) Rafael Nadal Docuseries ‘Rafa’: How a Local Setting, Language and Intimate Lensing Set the Primetime Emmy Contender Apart Making its world premiere in Sarajevo’s documentary competition, Milcho Manchevski ’s “ Good People ” leaves the broader political context to the journalists. Arriving a little over thirty years since his auspicious debut, the muscular war drama “After the Rain,” nabbed Venice’s Golden Lion, this strikingly austere and undecorated film, which Manchevski self-funded, doesn’t cover the vast institutional failures that precipitated the incident and increased its casualties. Instead, it assembles over 20 first-hand accounts by victims and witnesses, bringing to life the tragedy’s harrowing timeline through testimonies entirely. The result is a haunting portrait of social collapse whose power is premised on the words and faces of survivors. Popular on Variety Bookended by drone shots of the Macedonian countryside and a somber cello refrain by Novogradska, this 86-minute doc is otherwise composed of scoreless interviews with subjects seated in front of black curtains and captured in medium range. (Two brief exceptions include silent, phone-recorded footage of, first, the spark on the ceiling prior to the full break-out, and, second, an outside view of the club obscured by plumes of smoke.) The simplicity of the setup simplicity pays respect to the memory of the fallen, refusing to sensationalize the events or cater to morbid curiosity — principles that have dictated a long tradition of documentary filmmaking that privileges oral testimony, like Claude Lanzmann’s “Shoah” and Chantal Akerman’s “Tell Me.” But unlike those long take-heavy films, “Good People” cuts frequently between its subjects, a chorus-like effect that is sometimes choppy as editor Mishko Chunikhin flits between longer memories and observations as short as a few words. The doc starts out by describing the club’s downward spiral, with survivors — some of whose burn marks you can observe on their necks and hands — sharing eerily similar experiences. The beginning of the fire was widely mistaken as a special effect put on by the pop group performing at the time, and the flames spread quicker than clubbers could realize what was happening. “My eyes were seeing so many things that my brain couldn’t process,” says one of the more eloquent speakers, a young woman with shell-shocked eyes and flat-ironed hair who lost all of her friends in the incident. Proceeding chronologically through the night, the speakers recall navigating the chaos of people rushing toward the exit; and how this fatal stampede, along with asphyxiating conditions, knocked people unconscious, creating a “carpet of dead kids” under which more people were trapped and sometimes killed by suffocation, all while “burning alive.” Frequent fades to black and plain intertitles, displaying pithy phrases drawn from the interviews (like “that’s it” and “like helpless animals”), allow for moments of silence, encouraging the subjects’ words to soak in. These pauses also give the documentary an air of mournful respect, making its pace more deliberate than the standard talking heads-doc that might be mistaken as a stylistic counterpart. The second half introduces some parents of survivors and interviews with a handful of locals and early escapees who (re-)entered the club to help pull out injured bodies. The doc’s tagline — “when good people burn in hell” — comes off more than a bit crude, but the descriptions of people running out of the club burned and naked, their clothes and shoes torn off in the push to escape; or victims with bodies hot to the touch, their skin melting and ripping off the bone as rescuers pull them out from beneath piles of corpses, certainly justifies the metaphor. Against expectation, the film eschews neat narratives about survival and heroism. Ethics and normal human behavior are subsumed by “pure animal instinct” and “kicking, clawing, and biting.” If this doesn’t seem like a gracious revelation, there’s a point to the deep horror that Manchevski draws out here. As one subject explains, she feels “indignity” to have been violated so deeply by what she endured and witnessed. “Good People” may not explore the structural inadequacies that allowed this catastrophe to happen, but it does remind us of the ease with which our modern world can slide back into medieval times — and the responsibility we have to prevent it. ‘Good People’ Review: Milcho Manchevski’s Haunting Documentary Revisits the Kočani Nightclub Fire Through Survivors’ Eyes Reviewed at Sarajevo Film Festival (Competition), Aug. 15, 2026. title: Icelandic Producer Hlín Jóhannsdóttir Sets ‘Just a Kid’ With Alief Ahead of Haugesund and Reunites With ‘Driving Mum’ Team (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Aug 21, 2026 12:00am PT Icelandic Producer Hlín Jóhannsdóttir Sets ‘Just a Kid’ With Alief Ahead of Haugesund and Reunites With ‘Driving Mum’ Team (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Just a Kid,’ by newcomer Vala Ómarsdóttir, is co-produced by ‘Smoke Sauna Sisterhood’’s Alexandra Film in Estonia By Annika Pham Plus Icon Annika Pham Latest Haugesund New Nordic Films Reveals Standout 36 Nordic Projects and 15 Fresh Pics Set to Woo 300 Industry Attendees 1 week ago Haugesund New Nordic Films Unveils French Focus Including a Case Study on ‘Ibelin,’ From ‘The Imitation Game’ Director Morten Tyldum (EXCLUSIVE) 2 weeks ago Erik Poppe’s ‘Beloved’ to Open Haugesund: ‘All Eyes Are on Norway,’ Says Festival Chief Tonje Hardersen 3 weeks ago See All 'Just a Kid' Courtesy of Ursus Parvus Veteran Icelandic producer Hlín Jóhannsdóttir of Ursus Parvus, behind titles from some Iceland’s most renowned filmmakers including Fridrik Thor Fridriksson, Dagur Kári and Rúnar Rúnarsson, has signed with French-U.K. sales outfit Alief on the coming-of-age “Just a Kid” (“Bara barn”) by up-and-coming writer-director Vala Ómarsdóttir. To be pitched at New Nordic Films’ Works in Progress in Haugesund , Aug. 27, the project fits into Jóhannsdóttir’s roster of debut features by talented female directors, next to “Quake” by Tinna Hrafnsdóttir, which Alief sold to more than 20 territories including Juno Films in the U.S. Related Stories China Box Office: 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Retains Crown as 'Once Upon a Time in the Middle East,' 'The Odyssey' Surge in Previews 'The Odyssey' Star Samantha Morton 'Hasn't Worked for a Year' After Making Nolan's Epic Because 'I'm 49' Years Old and 'There's Other Good Actors Out There' Hlín Jóhannsdóttir, Hilmar Oddsson , Þröstur Leó Gunnarsson and Hera Hilmar Credit: Ursus Parvus Besides Alief, which chipped in an Minimum Guarantee, a strong partner on the project is Estonian producer Marianne Ostrat of Alexandra Film, producer of Sundance winner and Estonian Oscar entry ” Smoke Sauna Sisterhood ,” co-produced by Ursus Parvus. Popular on Variety In “Just a Kid,” the story turns on 16-year old Julia (Birgitta Marín Thorsdottir) who’s moved from Norway to Iceland and struggles to balance caring for her younger sister with fitting in at a new school. Drawn to charismatic Salka (Hafrún Arna Levy from “When the Light Breaks In”) and the school newspaper, she begins to find her voice. But when a traumatic drunken night resurfaces, Júlía must confront shame, family responsibilities and the courage to tell her own story, reads the logline. Speaking with Variety , the versatile filmmaker and performer Ómarsdóttir said the idea for the pic developed when she was pregnant with her second daughter. “I remember thinking about this bond we have, knowing that at some point when [my kids] get older they will not need me as much as they do now. I am very interested in this mother-daughter bond, especially concerning the teenage years,” said the helmer. After researching “what it feels like being a teenager today,” Ómarsdóttir said she drew from the rehearsal-driven sessions with her young cast “to continue the research, understand, and tell the story from their point of view.” “The whole experience was a long and exciting journey where I learned and discovered so many things. Both in visual storytelling and in human nature regarding the need to connect with someone and the need to set boundaries,” she said. Alief partner Miguel Govea who boarded the pic at development stage said “the story and setting drew us in. Once we saw the rehearsals, and proof of concept, we knew Hlin [Hrafnsdóttir] and Vala [Ómarsdóttir] had concocted some magic.” Boiling down the story and audience appeal he added: “Just a Kid” is a tender story of teen-angst and sexual awakening with a handsome cast that will resonate with discerning audiences.” “Just a Kid” received funding from the Icelandic Film Centre, Icelandic tax rebates, RÚV, Saga Film, Studio Syrland, Nordisk Film & TV Fond, and Estonian tax rebates. Max will handle the theatrical release in Iceland. “ Driving Mum ” Team In Haugesund, Jóhannsdóttir will also pitch at the Nordic Co-Production Market another project very close to her heart: “At The End of the Road,” which reunites her with the core team of the Tallinn Grand Prix winner “ Driving Mum :” writer/director Hilmar Oddsson, prominent actor Þröstur Leó Gunnarsson (“Noi the Albino,” “Solitude”) and Hera Hilmar (“Mortal Engines,” “Life in a Fishbowl”). In it, Leó, a renowned geriatrician specialized in Alzheimer’s disease, develops an unconventional friendship with Ásdís, a psychiatrist who’s returned to Iceland to care for her ailing grandmother. When Ásdís discovers that Leó himself is developing Alzheimer’s, both are forced to confront buried secrets. Jóhannsdóttir said she contributed to the development process with Oddsson and Gunnarsson as all have personal experiences about Alzheimer’s. “Sitting together, the three of us, and discussing the script was among the most rewarding experiences of my career as a creative producer,” she told Variety , underlining that the tone will remain darkly humorous. “I think a lot of people familiar with the disease will relate to the tragi-comedic side of Alzheimer’s.” “At the End of the Road” will “hopefully be both funny and dramatic, poetic, dreamlike, and realistic all at once,” said Oddsson in a statement. In Haugesund, Jóhannsdóttir will be looking for co-producers, co-financiers, sales and distribution. Commenting on the fact that “Just and Kid” and “At the End of the Road” are the only Icelandic projects selected for the popular the Norwegian Intl. Film Festival’s New Nordic Films showcase (Aug. 25-28) at Haugesund, the seasoned producer, who sat on the board of the Icelandic Producers Association for several years, said “things are very difficult in Iceland, funding-wise.” Citing the important Aug. 29 Icelandic referendum on whether to resume EU membership talks, she said: “our small nation is split, but it is really important for us producers that people at least to say ‘yes’ to the negotiations.” Karan Johar Hails ‘Unpredictable Nature’ of ‘The Traitors’ India as Season 2 Becomes Prime Video’s No. 1 Non-English Title (EXCLUSIVE) Ted Sarandos Meets Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Unveils Netflix India Storytelling Initiative India’s Paid Music Subscribers Could Hit 30 Million by 2028, EY-IMI Report Finds Cricket Rules India’s Streaming Viewership in New Ormax StreamView Report Buzz Title ‘Third Wheel,’ an ‘Allegory of Post-Colonial Africa,’ Brought to Market at Fantasia’s Frontières (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Macbeth,’ ‘Gaslit,’ ‘Silent Rebellion’ Win Raindance Awards With ‘Serena’ Winning Inaugural Best Horror Prize Loading comments... title: Billy Bob Thornton Says “Holly­wood Wasn’t Nice” to Taylor Sheridan, But That “Texas Accepted” Him
full_text: × Skip to main content By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All August 20, 2026 9:32pm Billy Bob Thornton and Taylor Sheridan Matei Horvath/Getty Images; Richard Rodriguez/Getty Images for Paramount Billy Bob Thornton is opening up about how he feels Texas embraced prolific TV creator Taylor Sheridan unlike Los Angeles. During a recent interview with Town & Country for a cover story about Sheridan, the Landman star said, “Holly­wood wasn’t nice to Taylor. There’s something about being an outsider that drives you.” Prior to building his television empire, which includes hit shows from Yellowstone and Mayor of Kingstown to Landman and Special Ops: Lioness , Sheridan was a struggling actor living in L.A. Related Stories TV 'Stranger Things' and 'The Pitt' Were the Most Streamed Original Series in the First Half of 2026 TV Taylor Sheridan Returning for an On-Camera Role in 'Lioness' Season 3 “I was homeless twice,” he said. “I lived in my car. Sometimes I’d go to Ojai, just somewhere where I could safely sleep. I did that for six months.” Despite the challenges, Sheridan said he “chose to sleep in my car” rather than giving up on his dream. However, after spending roughly two decades as a working actor, appearing on shows like Sons of Anarchy and Veronica Mars , his dream slightly changed when he pivoted to screenwriting — ultimately changing his life. Sheridan told The Hollywood Reporter during a 2023 cover story , “Hollywood will tell you what you’re supposed to do if you listen. If you’re banging your head against the wall for 20 years trying to be an actor, maybe you shouldn’t be an actor. But the first thing I ever wrote [the pilot for Mayor of Kingstown in 2011] got me meetings at every major network, at every agency. I had multiple people trying to buy it.” Once he gathered enough money from his early hits, such as Yellowstone , Sheridan decided to return to Texas, where he spent most of his childhood. He started buying up land and now owns more than 250,000 acres of ranchland across Texas, which includes his Four Sixes (6666) Ranch and Bosque Ranch. Thornton told Town & Country , “I think the ranch community in Texas accepted Taylor 100 percent because he’s not phoning it in. He doesn’t go to the tourist cowboy shop and get an outfit. This is the real thing.” Sheridan now spends most of his time in Texas, as he often invites castmembers to come to his ranch for meetings rather than going back to L.A. The ranching empire he’s built has also given him a creative edge, influencing the stories he writes that audiences love. “When I lived in Los Angeles, everything I saw was the same and I didn’t learn anything in my day-to-day life,” Sheridan previously told THR . “Here, I get to experience so much. I heard 25 iconic pieces of dialogue today. Most of my great lines I heard someone else say, or some version of it. I’m banking story all the time.” THR

title: Chris Hansen Didn’t Watch ‘Primetime’ Screening Because “A24 Wanted Me to Sign Away My Rights”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All August 20, 2026 8:36pm Chris Hansen Jason Mendez/Getty Images Chris Hansen said he didn’t watch an early screening of Robert Pattinson ‘s Primetime because he claimed that “A24 wanted me to sign away my rights.” During an interview on Fox News’ Jesse Watters Primetime Thursday evening, the former To Catch a Predator host said he went to the indie production studio and distributor’s office earlier in the day for a private screening of the film, but ended up leaving without seeing it. “The lawyers at A24 wanted me to sign away my rights to my name, image and brand, essentially, as well as any potential legal rights that would come out of the movie,” Hansen alleged. “I couldn’t sign that, so they didn’t show me the film. I went all the way over there. … But who’s going to sign something like that?” Related Stories Movies Chris Hansen Questions "Hollywood's Motive" With 'Primetime,' Says He'd Have Cast Denis Leary Movies 'Possession' Remake With Callum Turner, Margaret Qualley Sets Summer 2027 Release He added that it was a “very restrictive agreement” and that he “had never seen anything quite like it.” The Hollywood Reporter learned that Hansen was asked to sign a standard NDA a week in advance that all preview audiences must sign in order to watch an unreleased A24 film. It’s mostly to prevent spoilers and protect the studio’s IP. Hansen noted to Jesse Watters that his “lawyers had already seen” the NDA before he arrived at A24’s offices. When asked by the host what A24 might be worried about, the veteran journalist replied, “I don’t know! I haven’t seen the film. If you look at the trailer, obviously it’s a very dramatized version. They had told me that it’s fictionalized in many aspects. I know other people have seen it who didn’t sign an NDA, and yet they wanted me to sign it.” Primetime , which stars Pattinson as the Dateline NBC correspondent, chronicles the intense production, ethical dilemmas and media sensationalism behind To Catch a Predator , which ran from 2004 to 2007. During an interview with podcaster Annie Elise last week, Hansen questioned “Hollywood’s motive” behind the movie directed by Lance Oppenheim, but refused to judge the film until he’s seen it. “A couple months ago, they came and said, ‘Hey look, we’re doing this, we’d like you to have some sort of consideration in terms of helping us with this,'” he said. However, Hansen noted that the film was already made before “they” reached out to him. “As a reporter, it’s sort of silly for me to talk about something that I haven’t seen yet,” he added. “My suspicion is that they used my name because it helps in a commercial enterprise.” Primetime , also starring Merritt Wever, Skyler Gisondo, Phoebe Bridgers, Matthew Maher and Bokeem Woodbine, hits theaters on Sept. 25. title: Neon Sets Early Premium-Format Release for Na Hong-jin’s ‘Hope’ (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Patrick Brzeski Plus Icon Patrick Brzeski Asia Bureau Chief View All August 20, 2026 8:24pm Megabox has a lot riding on the local release of Na Hong-jin's 'Hope' later this month. Neon/Courtesy Everett Collection Logo text Neon is giving Korean action maestro Na Hong-jin ‘s gritty monster epic Hope an early theatrical launch on premium screens across the U.S. The distributor revealed Thursday that it will hold large-format screenings of Hope on Sept. 7 at 175 premium locations ahead of its wide release on Sept. 9. The one-night event, with showtimes at 6:30 p.m., spans six formats — Dolby Cinema, 4DX, ScreenX, Barco HDR, D-Box and Dolby Atmos — at theaters in New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, San Francisco, Dallas and elsewhere. The launch strategy is reminiscent of Neon’s rollout last year of Osgood Perkins’ The Monkey , which used advance premium-format screenings to build word of mouth on the way to the film’s strong $40 million theatrical performance. Related Stories TV Harry and Meghan Are Leaving California -- But Are They Leaving Hollywood? Music Why 'A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms' Broke One of 'Game of Thrones' Biggest Musical Rules One of the buzziest films to emerge from this year’s Cannes Film Festival, Hop e’s visceral spectacle certainly seems to warrant the premium-format splash. Describing the film as “a superbly sustained pedal-to-the-metal experience that’s almost dizzying in its bravura,” The Hollywood Reporter ‘s chief film critic hailed Hope as a “rip-roaring sci-fi creature feature” that “has instant cult classic written all over it.” Set in the fictional border town of Hope Harbor near the Korean Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), the film follows put-upon police chief Bum-seok (Hwang Jung-min) and his bad-ass female deputy Sung-ae ( Squid Game ‘s Hoyeon) as they frantically hunt an enormous mystery creature that has begun rampaging through their village. A band of local hunters, led by the charismatic Sung-ki (Zo In-sung), joins the chase and tracks the beast into a nearby forest — only to become its prey. What begins as a series of understandable misjudgments soon spirals into tragedy on a cosmic scale. Hope is Na’s first feature in roughly a decade. The writer-director has become a favorite of both arthouse fans and action aficionados thanks to his trio of stunning genre movies, the brutal crime thrillers The Chaser and The Yellow Sea and the 2016 horror sensation The Wailing . He reunites here to stunning effect with his Wailing cinematographer, Hong Kyung-pyo, a revered figure in the Korean industry whose other credits include Bong Joon Ho’s Parasite and Lee Chang-dong’s Burning . Hope ‘s score is by Michael Abels, the composer behind Jordan Peele’s Get Out and Nope . The film’s Korean ensemble is rounded out by surprising supporting characters played by Michael Fassbender, Alicia Vikander, Taylor Russell and Cameron Britton. Hope opened at home in South Korea on July 15 and has earned $35 million, becoming the country’s third-biggest domestic release this year. Na conceived Hope as the first chapter of a potential franchise — and, so far, international distributors appear on board. The film’s main backer and sales agent, Plus M pre-sold the title to roughly 200 territories out of Cannes, a record for a Korean film, with the deals reportedly recouping nearly half of the movie’s net production budget ahead of release. title: Chris Hansen Says He Refused to Sign His Rights Away in Order to Screen Robert Pattinson’s ‘Primetime’
full_text: Aug 20, 2026 6:43pm PT Chris Hansen Says He Refused to Sign His Rights Away in Order to Screen Robert Pattinson’s ‘Primetime’ By Clayton Davis Plus Icon Clayton Davis Chief Awards Editor byClaytonDavis Latest Chris Hansen Says He Refused to Sign His Rights Away in Order to Screen Robert Pattinson’s ‘Primetime’ 8 hours ago David Harbour Talks Learning ASL for ‘DTF St. Louis,’ Shares a Line From ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ and Wants a Christopher Nolan-Directed ‘Warcraft’ Movie 2 days ago Dale Dickey on Her First Emmy Nomination for ‘Widow’s Bay’ and the Monologue That Made Her Say, ‘What the F—‘ 3 days ago See All Getty / A24 Chris Hansen didn’t get to take a seat for the new A24 movie “ Primetime .” The 66-year-old veteran journalist went to the offices of indie distributor A24 to watch the Lance Oppenheim film, in which he is played by Robert Pattinson , before it bows at the Venice Film Festival. But he left without seeing it. The former “To Catch a Predator” host went on Fox News’ “Jesse Watters Primetime” to say he showed up at the studio’s offices for a 10 a.m. private screening of “Primetime” on Thursday. The Pattinson-led drama is built around Hansen’s run atop the hidden-camera franchise. But Hansen claims he walked away after refusing to sign a legal agreement he describes as unlike anything he has encountered in four decades on the beat. Related Stories China Box Office: 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Retains Crown as 'Once Upon a Time in the Middle East,' 'The Odyssey' Surge in Previews 'The Odyssey' Star Samantha Morton 'Hasn't Worked for a Year' After Making Nolan's Epic Because 'I'm 49' Years Old and 'There's Other Good Actors Out There' A source close to A24 said Hansen was asked to sign a standard NDA that all preview audiences must adhere to for an unreleased film — mostly to prevent spoilers and protect the studio’s IP. Popular on Variety “The lawyers at A24 wanted me to sign away my rights to my name, image and brand essentially, as well as any potential legal rights that would come out of the movie,” Hansen claimed during the appearance. “I couldn’t sign that, so they didn’t show me the film. I went all the way over there.” Pressed by Watters on whether he walked in without legal cover, Hansen says his attorneys had already reviewed the paperwork and advised against signing. “Of course not,” he says when asked if he put his name to anything without a lawyer present. “This was a very restrictive agreement. I’ve never seen anything quite like it.” The agreement Hansen describes would be a much larger legal matter than a standard screening NDA, and would not be asked of other individuals screening the film — including press and third-party marketing agencies. The account marks a sharp turn from where Hansen left things only days earlier. Speaking on the “Serialously With Annie Elise” podcast, he said A24 was setting him up with a private screening “in the next week or so,” after which he would render a verdict on the film and how he felt about the depiction of his career. Robert Pattinson as Chris Hansen in A24’s “Primetime.” Courtesy of A24 Hansen says he cannot say what the studio might be worried about, because he still has not watched a minute of the picture. “I haven’t seen the film,” he says. “If you look at the trailer, obviously it’s a very dramatized version. They had told me that it’s fictionalized in many aspects. I know other people have seen it who didn’t sign an NDA, and yet they wanted me to sign it.” In the trailer and other marketing materials for the film, the indie distributor has labeled “Primetime” as “inspired by true events” and has not characterized it as a biopic of Hansen or his life. The film is written by Ajon Singh, one of Variety’s 10 Screenwriters to Watch from 2025 , and is inspired by “Tonight on Dateline This Man Will Die” by Luke Dittrich. Hansen is careful to note he is not chasing a payday. “I have no financial stake in this film,” he says, adding that no one from the production paid him or brought him aboard as a consultant. He learned the movie existed, he says, the way he has learned most things across a long career. “I’m just a working reporter, and I’m not learned in the sophisticated ways of Hollywood. But I find stuff out,” Hansen says. “I’ve been an investigative reporter for four decades, so I knew this was going on.” His frustration, he suggests, is less about the film than the timing of the outreach. “I get a call today saying, ‘Well, you know, everybody’s concerned. They want you to be happy with the film,'” Hansen says. “Well, then why didn’t you tell me about it when you started shooting the film?” “Primetime” opens in theaters Sept. 25 following its world premiere in competition at the Venice Film Festival. Directed by Oppenheim in his narrative feature debut and written by Ajon Singh, the movie follows Hansen in 2006 as “To Catch a Predator” makes the leap from “Dateline NBC” segment to its own primetime block. Pattinson stars and produces through his Icki Eneo Arlo banner, with a supporting cast that includes Merritt Wever, Skyler Gisondo, Phoebe Bridgers and Bokeem Woodbine. Former NBCUniversal chief Jeff Zucker appears as himself. “To Catch a Predator” ran from 2004 to 2007 as a recurring “Dateline NBC” investigation, pairing Hansen and a camera crew with decoys posing as minors to confront men who arrived at sting houses. The franchise was canceled after a 2006 Texas operation in which Rockwall County assistant district attorney Louis Conradt died by suicide as authorities and the show’s crew closed in on his home. For now, it looks like Hansen will have to see the movie the way the rest of the country will, with a paid theater ticket. Asked what he would say to Pattinson, he reaches, inevitably, for the line that made him famous. “Take a seat right over there,” Hansen says. A24 declined to comment. title: Trouble In Paradise: John Ross Bowie & Brian Posehn On Who Ruined Utopia In ‘Stuart Fails’ E5
full_text: Skip to main content By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie Trouble In Paradise: John Ross Bowie & Brian Posehn On Who Ruined Utopia In ‘Stuart Fails’ E5 ‘Outer Banks’ Creators Break Down Season 5’s “Earned” Ending, Supernatural Lean & JJ’s Presence Dave Bautista Set To Play Kratos In ‘God Of War’ As Amazon Series Recasts Lead View All August 20, 2026 6:30pm Brian Posehn, John Ross Bowie, Kevin Sussman in 'Stuart Fails To Save The Universe' ABC SPOILER ALERT: The story includes details about Episode 5 of HBO Max ‘s Stuart Fails To Save the Universe . In Episode 5 of Big Bang Theory spinoff Stuart Fails To Save the Universe, our quartet of inter-dimensional travelers Stuart Bloom ( Kevin Sussman ), Denise ( Lauren Lapkus ), Bert ( Brian Posehn ) and Barry Kripke ( John Ross Bowie ), land in a tropical paradise inhabited by a primitive tribe of scantly-clothed beautiful people living in a commune where they share everything — food, shelter, and sexual partners. All goes well until Kripke introduces the concept of possession and free market, leading to tribe members, who had been living in harmony, turning on each other and getting into fights, with him feigning innocence that he has no idea how the turmoil started. Related Stories Ratings 'Lanterns' Premieres Among HBO Max's Top Titles, Besting DC Studios Predecessor 'The Penguin' Casting 'The Pitt' Adds 7 To Season 3 Recurring Cast It’s probably fitting that it was Kripke who destroyed utopia. However, “Chuck brought up a point earlier today, saying that Bert has a little hand in that by bringing monogamy into their world, like maybe he should have never done that,” Posehn said in an interview with Deadline, referencing Chuck Lorre, co-creator of Stuart Fails To Save the Universe alongside Bill Prady and Zak Penn. Added Bowie, “Yeah, it’s funny because we have been collectively all blaming Kripke for introducing the free market to paradise, but yeah, Burt holds some responsibility for introducing monogamy as well.” In the episode, Bert is immediately propositioned by one of the gorgeous local women, who quickly becomes his girlfriend, stopping to sleep with others upon Bert’s request as they are headed to the altar. “It felt that episode was incredibly fun to shoot because we like joke-wise, it’s just one killer joke after another in that show,” Bowie said. “But also, it made kind of perfect sense that Kripke would be a big part of bringing down Utopia. And then the way that he completely shirked responsibility at the end — that sense of like, wow, what got into these guys? That was really great. And that cast, oh my God! They found all these beautiful people who were all really funny, all these like gorgeous people who would come in and land jokes, and it was incredible to watch.” Five episodes in, Bert has had the coolest arc of the main characters — from turning commando in Episode 1 to bring mayhem to Caltech and then kicking Kripke’s butt after he’d killed Raj, to doing magic and having a posse of adoring acolytes in Episode 3 to landing a stunning girlfriend in Episode 5. Posehn is loving it. “Well, just getting Bert to do more was already a dream,” he said. “But then the stuff they put me through in the first season was so fun. Every week there was something new, some new thing that I went home to my wife and said, ‘Holy shi*, you won’t believe what Bert’s doing this week.'” Added Bowie, “Well, you were both a fighter and a lover, and that was fun to watch.” Stuart Fails To Save The Universe has been renewed for a second season. title: ‘The Magic Faraway Tree’ Review: Claire Foy and Andrew Garfield in an Exhaustingly Cutesy Kid Flick
full_text: × Skip to main content By Frank Scheck Plus Icon Frank Scheck View All August 20, 2026 4:32pm 'The Magic Faraway Tree' Vertical Plenty of British children’s stories have managed to catch on with American audiences via their cinematic adaptations, from Mary Poppins to Charlie and the Chocolate Factory to Paddington . The latest entry to cross the pond is unlikely to reap similar success despite the presence of Claire Foy and Andrew Garfield in leading roles and a supporting cast featuring some of England’s finest thespians. Adapted from Enid Blyton’s 1943 novel, which was part of a three-book series, The Magic Faraway Tree proves so relentlessly twee and sugary that all but the youngest viewers will find themselves at risk of a diabetic coma. Related Stories Movies 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Aims to Swing Past 'Insidious' Sequel for Fourth Box Office Win Movies Danny Boyle's Rupert Murdoch Movie 'Ink' Sets December Theatrical Release From Netflix Foy and Garfield play Polly and Tim, a married couple who decide to decamp from their London home when Polly resigns from her job at a manufacturing company after said company installs spying technology in the smart refrigerator — voiced by Judi Dench , of all people — that she’s invented. So they take off with their kids to the rural countryside, renting a dilapidated barn and creating a tomato farm to fulfill Tim’s dream of marketing his homemade pasta sauce. The Magic Faraway Tree The Bottom Line Too imaginative for its own good. Release date : Friday, August 21 Cast : Claire Foy, Andrew Garfield, Nonso Anozie, Nicola Coughlan, Delilah Bennett-Cardy, Billie Gadsdon, Phoenix Laroche, Dustin Demri-Burns, Jessica Gunning, Hiran Abeysekera, Mark Heap, Pippa Bennett-Warner, Oliver Chris, Lenny Henry, Michael Palin, Simon Russell Beale, Jennifer Saunders, Rebecca Ferguson Director : Ben Gregor Screenwriter: Simon Farnaby Rated PG, 1 hour 50 minutes The decision doesn’t sit well with their three children: smartphone-obsessed Beth (Delilah Bennett-Cardy), who is horrified to discover that their new home doesn’t include electricity and running water, let alone Wi-Fi; and younger siblings Joe (Phoenix Laroche) and mostly silent Fran (Billie Gadsdon). “I don’t understand, have we gone back in time?” Joe plaintively asks. Their feelings change when Fran has an encounter with Silky (Nicola Coughlan of Bridgerton ), an exuberant fairy, who invites her to join her for tea at the Magic Faraway Tree. There, a newly verbal Fran meets a variety of bizarre characters including the aptly named Moonface (Nonso Anozie); the Saucepan Man (Dustin Demri-Burns), who’s clad in kitchen paraphernalia; Dame Washalot (Jessica Gunning of Baby Reindeer ), who, yes, does a lot of scrubbing; and Mr. Whatzisname (Oliver Chris), who, you guessed it, has memory issues. Not so magical complications ensue, with the overstuffed proceedings eventually involving such other fantastical characters as the Birthday Elves, who offer each of the children one wish (Joe asks to be turned into his favorite Minecraft character, which is presumably an update from the original story); Mr. Oom Boom Boom (Mark Heap), who has the handy ability to reverse the wishes; and the Know-Alls (Michael Palin, Lenny Henry, Simon Russell Beale, all virtually unrecognizable under mounds of facial hair). It’s all, as you can imagine, more than a bit much, and by the time the villainess Dame Snap (Rebecca Ferguson, whose giant lopsided wig probably required her to see a chiropractor between takes) comes along, you find yourself rooting for her. Indeed, it’s the most acerbic characters who prove the most endearing, especially the children’s grandmother played by British national treasure Jennifer Saunders , who practically makes a meal out of her disgusted exclamation, “Unemployed!” Screenwriter Simon Farnaby has plenty of experience with this sort of material, having co-written the screenplays for Paddington 2 and Wonka , but he doesn’t bring similar wit to these proceedings. He also shows up briefly as a friendly farmer who provides the opportunity for a labored gag in which he confuses “Wi-Fi” for “wifey.” And while Foy is appealing as the indefatigable mother, Garfield leans too heavily into manic cutesiness as the endlessly chirpy father who at times seems less grown-up than his children. The story’s ultimate message about the kids learning to forego their electronic devices to embrace the joy of friends and family also seems a bit ironic, considering the film’s future as an electronic babysitter. The Magic Faraway Tree is most notable for the imaginative costume and make-up designs for its outlandish characters and the brightly colored, pastel visuals that give you the feeling you’re looking at an oversized children’s book. But even the distinctive look becomes wearisome after not too long. By the time the film is over, you’ll be longing for some refreshing monochrome. Full credits Production: Palisades Park Pictures, Neal Street, Elysian Film Group Distributor: Vertical Cast: Claire Foy, Andrew Garfield, Nonso Anozie, Nicola Coughlan, Delilah Bennett-Cardy, Billie Gadsdon, Phoenix Laroche, Dustin Demri-Burns, Jessica Gunning, Hiran Abeysekera, Mark Heap, Pippa Bennett-Warner, Oliver Chris, Lenny Henry, Michael Palin, Simon Russell Beale, Jennifer Saunders, Rebecca Ferguson Director: Ben Gregor Screenwriter: Simon Farnaby Producers: Pippa Harris, Nicholas Brown, Danny Perkins, Jane Hooks Executive producers: Amara Birkemoe, Michael Cornelius, Jacqueline De Croy, Simon Williams, Joe Simpson, Merrick Stoller, Andy Wang, Matthew Chausse Director of photography: Zac Nicholson Production designer: Alexandra Walker Editor: Gary Dollner Composer: Isabella Summers Costume designer: Ann Maskrey Casting: Lucinda Syson, Natasha Vincent, Verity Naughton Rated PG, 1 hour 50 minutes THR
