title: ‘Lanterns’ EP Damon Lindelof Weighs In on 2026’s Adaptation Wars: “Shouldn’t We Be Beyond This by Now?”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Brian Davids Plus Icon Brian Davids Writer PickYourBrian Follow Sign Up View All August 20, 2026 3:59pm Aaron Pierre in Lanterns John Johnson/HBO Max Logo text If you’re terminally online, you’ve probably found yourself swept up in this year’s exhausting discourse over creative license and beloved IP. When the now well-received Lanterns premiered its official trailer earlier this year, a vocal subset of fans objected to the premise of taking the ring-powered space cops of the Green Lantern Corps and grounding these colorful, cosmic superheroes in small-town Nebraska for a desaturated, Taylor Sheridan-esque riff on True Detective . Earth’s first Green Lantern, Hal Jordan, played by Kyle Chandler , also drew criticism for being portrayed as an older, messier iteration of the most famous intergalactic peacekeeper rather than the more idealized version in his prime. Related Stories TV 'Lanterns' Premiere Lights Up Strong Ratings on HBO, HBO Max Movies 'The Odyssey' Beats 'Deadpool & Wolverine' to Become Biggest R-Rated Movie Ever Concurrently, Christopher Nolan ’s modernized adaptation of Homer’s ancient Greek poem, The Odyssey , endured endless kvetching prior to becoming the highest-grossing film of his storied career. Some found fault with the use of American accents instead of British ones, something Hollywood has long conditioned audiences to hear in sword-and-sandal epics. Others argued that the characters should be speaking with Greek accents or even in an ancient Greek dialect to honor the source material’s roots in Greek mythology. Additional gripes, among many others, targeted the use of the word “dad,” the Greek soldiers’ anachronistic armor and two casting choices that together accounted for less than ten minutes of screen time. Resident Evil writer-director Zach Cregger — who delivered two of the most unique genre films this decade, Barbarian and the Oscar-winning Weapons — has also taken a great deal of flak for having the audacity to tell a new story that’s set inside the world of the popular video game franchise. Hardcore Resident Evil devotees contend that he should have just made an original movie if he didn’t want to meaningfully engage with the existing characters and stories. Cregger maintains that his goal was to capture the experience of playing the games he himself loves. If anyone understands fan backlash and demands for adaptational fidelity, it’s Lanterns ‘ Emmy-winning co-creator Damon Lindelof . He’s worked across a wide range of existing IP, including Watchmen , Star Trek , Star Wars , Alien , World War Z and The Leftovers . He also co-created Lost , a series that is bound to be revisited or reinterpreted by someone else down the road. Having lived on both sides of the equation, he has heard every possible reaction to his work, from effusive praise to deep-seated contempt. “We all just have to acknowledge that there’s a level of hubris involved in taking on any of this preexisting IP. But it is called adaptation. Source material is supposed to change and evolve [by definition],” Lindelof tells The Hollywood Reporter . “As a consumer and as someone who’s making this stuff, there’s almost a responsibility to take risks. I don’t think anybody wants to see you be completely and totally vigilant to the source material because then it isn’t an adaptation at all. Shouldn’t we be beyond this conversation by now?” While some of these perpetual controversies are generated with financial and/or political incentive in mind, Lindelof notes that such grievances are partially tied to Hollywood’s habit of returning to the same wells. And though consumers claim to want more brand-new experiences like Obsession , the numbers continue to show that branded entertainment still rules the day. “There is a fundamental grumbling and annoyance that we’re still telling the same stories over and over and over again. But at the same time, we’re hungry for something new,” Lindelof says. “And because we don’t want to resolve or acknowledge that paradox in ourselves, we throw it onto the culture. It manifests itself in conversations about whether or not Odysseus is having enough sex.” Thus, until the audience behavior truly shifts away from franchise stories, barring a few outliers each year, creators like Lindelof will keep utilizing creative license to reimagine the familiar in the most compelling ways possible. “Nobody who does what we do goes to bed at night, saying, ‘All that I care about is whether or not I pissed off the fans.’ They go to bed at night, going, ‘Did I do anything worthwhile creatively? Did I put anything authentically emotional into this story that people can relate to?’” Lindelof says. “And the fact that we have to do it inside familiar IP most of the time is the cost of doing business.” Below, during a conversation with THR , Lindelof and fellow Lanterns co-creator Tom King also discuss the inspiration behind the traumatic backstory of aspiring Green Lantern, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), as well as the challenge King currently faces in adapting his 2017 Mister Miracle comic book run for animation. *** It’s nothing new, but the discourse this year surrounding adaptations and source material has been as insufferable as it’s ever been. Whether it’s Lanterns or The Odyssey or Resident Evil , there’s been so much bellyaching over creative license. Some of it is manufactured and disingenuous, but why do you think there’s so much resistance to change when it’s been proven that people rarely want more of the same? DAMON LINDELOF I love the frame on the question. I love how insufferable [the discourse] is, and at the same time, it feels like it’s such a vital conversation. In the case of The Odyssey , which is millennia-old, or Green Lantern [comic series], which is on the right side of the century mark, our engagement in these works generates a high level of passion. But the other level of it is this weird conceptual framework of ownership, and that’s where it becomes insufferable. There’s a direct corollary to the amount of time that you spend ingesting something or thinking about something or talking about it with your friends or communities. You begin to feel like a proprietary interest in protecting it. So I think we all just have to acknowledge that there’s a level of hubris involved in taking on any of this preexisting IP. But to your point, it is called adaptation. I don’t have my dictionary handy, and while I’m sure there are multiple definitions of adaptation, the one that resonates the most for me is that source material is supposed to change and evolve. [ Writer’s Note: To his point, here’s another definition: Something that is changed or modified to suit new conditions or needs. ] The fandom will also watch the new Harry Potter trailer and be like, “This just looks exactly like Harry Potter .” And then the other side of the fandom is like, “Thank God, this is exactly what I want. This is what I love about Harry Potter .” When you try to split that difference and say, “How can we do something original inside something that is iterative [and/or] older than God?” — that is always the $64,000 question. I should probably add inflation. The answer, particularly in the case for Tom and I, is that we identify primarily as fans. We were fans of this content long before we got the opportunity to make it. You don’t start from a place of, What would I do ? You start from a place of, What would excite me? What would I hate? Then you always come to an answer that’s going to have some risk involved. As a consumer and as someone who’s making this stuff, there’s almost a responsibility to take risks. It’s not just for the sake of taking them; you’ve got to earn them. I don’t think anybody wants to see you be completely and totally vigilant to the source material because then it isn’t an adaptation at all. Aaron Pierre ‘s John Stewart in Lanterns John Johnson/HBO Max Tom, what’s your take on this tug of war? TOM KING To me, at the end of the day, it’s quality. And that’s such a stupid answer. Clueless , which is an adaptation of Jane Austen’s Emma , is completely different. It almost has nothing to do with it, but it’s such a good movie on its own. When you look into it and you see the Jane Austen of it all, you’re like, Oh my God, that’s an amazing adaptation . So adaptations have to do two things at once: they have to stand on their own and they have to talk to the old material. If they can’t stand on their own, then what you’re going to see is how you misinterpreted the old material. So quality, quality, quality is always just the apex of everything. When artists or bands cover well-known songs, the whole point is to hear their twist on the material. Nobody expected Johnny Cash’s “Hurt” to be a carbon copy of Nine Inch Nails’ original, so it’s puzzling to me why movie and TV adaptations are held to a different standard. LINDELOF I hard agree. I also don’t even know if they’re being held to any standard at all. There is a fundamental grumbling and annoyance that we’re still telling the same stories over and over and over again. But at the same time, we’re hungry for something new. And because we don’t want to resolve or acknowledge that paradox in ourselves, we throw it onto the culture. It manifests itself in conversations about whether or not Odysseus is having enough sex. KING So you do open my emails. Good. LINDELOF & KING ( Laugh .) LINDELOF But I do find the conversation much more exhilarating on the outside than from the inside. Also, look at the movies and television shows that are generating the most interest and the most eyeballs. It’s disproportionately a retelling versus a telling. So when something fresh and original like Backrooms or Obsession comes along, it’s the exception to the rule versus the rule. All of us are completely and totally overwhelmed by the familiar. Nobody who does what we do goes to bed at night, saying, “All that I care about is whether or not I pissed off the fans.” They go to bed at night, going, “Did I do anything worthwhile creatively? Did I put anything authentically emotional into this story that people can relate to?” And the fact that we have to do it inside familiar IP most of the time is the cost of doing business. But I don’t disagree with you. Shouldn’t we be beyond this conversation by now? KING I’m working on Mister Miracle now, this animated series within the DC Universe. It’s me adapting myself, but it’s myself from ten years ago. LINDELOF The fans will get to say, “ You ruined it!” KING ( Laughs .) As a comic book writer, I’ve been to ten years of conventions where people tell me about the parts they loved and hated in the book. So I’ve been arguing with myself from ten years back, being like, Oh my God, you wrote that well , or, You wrote that terribly . I’m hearing those fans from conventions in my head, and I’m hearing my own instincts as a creator who’s learned a ton since then, including by watching Damon create. So all of this is entirely on my mind, and I’m trying to produce something that both honors and elevates the original on a new medium. Cairo Cash Lee as Young John Stewart in Lanterns John Johnson/HBO Max John Stewart’s (Aaron Pierre) traumatic backstory seems like it has both of your fingerprints all over it. LINDELOF & KING ( Laugh .) Actually, I could say the same thing about Hal. He has a little bit of Dogen (Hiroyuki Sanada’s Lost character) in his background. In the case of John, though, had one of you been dabbling in Swiss folklore at the time? LINDELOF In truth, a lot of that came from Vanessa [Baden Kelly], who wrote the [third] episode. Justin Britt-Gibson, as well. He was in our writers’ room, and we previously worked on a Star Wars movie that we never got to make. I don’t know how familiar you are with comic-book John’s myriad backstories and introductions, but it was this idea of trying to honor the inconsistency of his comic book legacy with some new ideas of our own. Obviously, I was really proud to be in this room. This is not a show that I ran; Chris Mundy ran it impeccably. So it felt like I was batting around .175 in terms of the ideas that I was throwing out. But the more exciting part of the job was hearing other ideas from the other writers and going, “Yes, that .” So when it came to John’s origin story, Tom pitched the dad and the apples, and that was very early in the pilot we wrote with Chris. But working backwards from that and saying, “Alright, how did we get here ?” — a lot of that heavy lifting came from Vanessa. KING Yeah, I remember us going, “This is a father story.” And she was like, “No, this is a mother story.” LINDELOF She was like, “Enough of the bad dads.” *** Lanterns is now airing new episodes on HBO/HBO Max every Sunday until Oct 4. THR

title: L.A. Mayoral Candidate Nithya Raman Says Legality of Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger “Should Be Decided in Court”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Katie Kilkenny Plus Icon Katie Kilkenny Enterprise Reporter, TV & Labor katiekilkenny7 Follow Sign Up View All August 20, 2026 3:40pm Los Angeles City Councilmember and mayoral candidate Nithya Raman speaks at a campaign event with volunteers and supporters on June 13 in North Hollywood. Mario Tama/Getty Images Los Angeles mayoral candidate Nithya Raman is sticking by her position that the legality of the Paramount – Warner Bros. Discovery merger should be decided in court. The sitting L.A. councilmember reiterated her support for California Attorney General Rob Bonta’s antitrust suit to block the $111 billion deal in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter on Thursday. “Los Angeles’ film industry is already in crisis. The Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger would deepen it, costing an estimated 4,500 film and television jobs, more than 10,000 jobs region-wide, and billions of dollars in economic activity, according to a new county report,” Raman said. “This is a bad deal for entertainment workers and a bad deal for Los Angeles. That’s why I support Attorney General Rob Bonta’s antitrust lawsuit and stand with the workers fighting this merger.” The councilmember added, “Paramount’s threat to leave California unless the lawsuit is dropped is an attempt to strong-arm our state. Serious questions about this merger’s legality should be decided in court, not through corporate threats.” Raman’s statement arrived on the same day that sitting Mayor Karen Bass held a press conference calling for a hasty resolution to the standoff between Bonta and Paramount Skydance. “It is time for all parties to come to the table. The continued uncertainty is not good for workers, not good for productions and not good for the future of this industry,” Bass said. The sitting mayor added that any solution must include enforceable commitments to keep Paramount and Warner Bros. based in L.A. and to retain jobs, film and TV shoots, and investment in California. In saying so, Bass followed the lead of movie theater trade group Cinema United as well as the DGA and IATSE, which also have recently asked the parties in the lawsuit to come together quickly and hash out their differences to avoid any further industry disruption. Raman and Bass are set to go toe-to-toe in the general election in November. While Bass has gained the support of some Hollywood crew unions and industry figures like J.J. Abrams and Samuel L. Jackson, Raman — whose husband, Vali Chandrasekaran, was a writer-producer on 30 Rock and Modern Family — has her own deep bench of Hollywood supporters, especially among writers and comedians. The mayoral candidates’ statements on the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery deal arrived just one day after the L.A. Department of Economic Opportunity and CVL Economics released a report detailing how thousands of jobs are at risk as a result of the proposed merger. THR

title: ‘Outer Banks’ Creators Break Down Season 5’s “Earned” Ending, Supernatural Lean & JJ’s Presence
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News California Film & TV Tax Credits In Peril As Sacramento Deal Falls Apart: Exclusive Read the full story By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie Trouble In Paradise: John Ross Bowie & Brian Posehn On Who Ruined Utopia In ‘Stuart Fails’ E5 ‘Outer Banks’ Creators Break Down Season 5’s “Earned” Ending, Supernatural Lean & JJ’s Presence Dave Bautista Set To Play Kratos In ‘God Of War’ As Amazon Series Recasts Lead View All August 20, 2026 3:35pm From left: Carlacia Grant, Jonathan Daviss, Madelyn Cline, Drew Starkey, Madison Bailey and Chase Stokes in 'Outer Banks' Netflix SPOILER ALERT: The story includes details about Season 5 of Netflix ‘s Outer Banks . There were a lot of full-circle elements in the fifth and final season of Outer Banks . The series ended the way it started, with a hurricane. Sarah (Madelyn Cline) wore a version of her iconic Midsummers white dress from Season 1 to her wedding to John B (Chase Stokes) in the series finale where the two recited the vows she used for their impromptu nuptials on the open seas in Season 2. And the Pogues, in the same lineup as their very first treasure hunt (sans the late JJ), went on one final adventure together in Azerbaijan. Related Stories News All The Songs In ‘Outer Banks’ Season 5: Tame Impala, Stevie Wonder & More News ‘Outer Banks’ Season 5 Finale: How Things End For Pogues, Kooks & Twinkie As John B & Co Sign Off It wasn’t your typical Outer Banks season: there were three proposals — two by Pope (Jonathan Daviss) to Cleo (Carlacia Grant), one by Rafe (Drew Starkey) to Sofia (Fiona Palomo), a wedding (Sarah and John B) and a baby, as the couple welcomed a son whom, as expected, they named JJ, after their beloved friend who was supposed to be the baby’s godfather. Watch on Deadline The show leaned into the supernatural, too, with Kiara, JJ’s father Chandler Groff (J. Anthony Crane) and rich collector Finch all chasing Blackbeard’s Blue Crown to try and resurrect a loved one: JJ; Groff’s wife (and JJ’s mother), whom he had killed; and Finch’s young daughter, respectively. (Groff also senselessly killed JJ, but he didn’t seem to feel remorse over that.) Holding the crown, Kiara did see JJ under a meteor shower, but it was her memories of him. The season also had a revenge thriller vibe as, in her grief, Kiara went full Kill Bill on Groff, chasing him down to murder him, which she did on her second try. Ultimately, it was a happy ending for the Pogues who were able to get back one of the many treasures they had discovered only to see them being taken away – the Royal Merchant gold — which they recovered from the ocean floor after the boat Groff and Kiara were on sunk in the hurricane. Kiara managed to stay afloat while waiting for the Pogues to rescue her as she found herself in calm waters under the eye of the storm. This was the second time she cheated death, having been sent to the bottom of the ocean by Groff in an earlier episode, summoning JJ for help both times. With the money from the gold, the Pogues “rebuilt the island the way it should be so all of us, Kooks and Pogues, could live there… forever,” as John B said at the end of the finale. On the new Kildare, Kooks largely bailed out, Pogues moved in, Pope and Cleo settled into his ancestral home, Tannyhill, and Topper is a bartender. In an interview with Deadline, Outer Banks creators Josh Pate , Jonas Pate and Shannon Burke discuss the ending, what parts of it they had conceived years ago and what elements they had added more recently. They also answer burning questions about the fate of some characters, including what happened to Rafe and Sofia, and whether Sarah and Rafe’s stepmother Rose got any of the gold she had kept until Groff stole it from her. Each Outer Banks character had their own ending, many of which converged at John B and Sarah’s wedding . The trio also explain whether they ever considered bringing JJ back from the dead or have Rudy Pankow reprise his role in any way, if they thought of killing off another Pogue and why Groff was so unredeemable. As part of the interview, Josh and Jonas Pate and Burke also revealed that a prequel set 20 years prior , which features the Outer Banks parents’ generation, is in active development at Netflix. “It really is the story of how the island split — and it’s particularly relevant in our country right now — how it split into the haves and have-nots, how the Kooks and the Pogues started,” Josh Pate said . “How did this rift start?” Below, they tease another possible spinoff. Ending on a Win DEADLINE: Let’s start with with the ending. You said after Season 4 that you’re “bringing it all home.” Is this what you envision, building a Kildare utopia with Kooks and Pogues living in harmony? JONAS PATE : Yes. JOSH PATE : I don’t think the Kooks are there anymore. I think the Kooks have all been kind of driven off. JONAS PATE : No, no, no. There are some, maybe we have a disagreement on that. But I think it’s the happiest ending you could possibly have. Everybody’s there living together. We had lost for 49 straight episodes, so we feel like we earned the happy ending. JOSH PATE : I agree. I think it’s a happy ending, and that’s what we wanted it to be — as happy as we could make it, given everything that had happened in the story. DEADLINE: Is this ending in the ballpark of what you had envisioned from the beginning, from when you created the show? BURKE : It is. Many elements of the final sequence, we discussed at the end of Season 1. DEADLINE: Like Sarah and John B’s wedding? BURKE : Yeah, all that. Tannyhill going to Pope. We sort of knew that it got some traction after Season 1, so we long-arced it from there. So we knew this is where we were going the whole time. JONAS PATE : And bookending with a hurricane, getting an ending with a hurricane. That was pretty much an original idea because [the series] starts with a hurricane. DEADLINE: I thought you were going to end it with the Pogues on the beach after the storm and recreate that power outage photo that became the inspiration for the show. Did you think about ending the series with that shot? JOSH PATE : No, that’s a good question, though. I wish you’d been around. That’s a great idea. JONAS PATE : Do you want to be on the writers staff for the prequel? DEADLINE: Was there anything in the ending that changed from the way you had originally planned it? JOSH PATE : I think Rafe was a big change. I don’t think that at the beginning we had thought that Rafe would be as big a character as he became, as much as we started to really like Drew. Would you guys say that’s fair? I think that evolved. JONAS PATE : Yeah, and I’d say Pope and Cleo. Both of them had real distinct journeys over this year particularly and I would say that that is more reacting to what happened to Pope in the final episode of the last season and just following it through. Drew Starkey as Rafe in ‘Outer Banks’ Season 5 Jackson Lee Davis/Netflix Where in the World Is Rafe? DEADLINE: Speaking of Rafe, was it deliberate that we never heard from him again? He was supposed to send the gang a postcard from Rio, that didn’t happen. He and Sofia left literally with just the shirts on their backs. Where are they? Are they in South America? JOSH PATE : That is another spinoff possibility. JONAS PATE : In the credits, you see a video call from Rafe at the wedding. DEADLINE: Yes, but we still didn’t get an update. Did he and Sofia get a cut from the gold? JOSH PATE : Good question. I don’t know. We sort of felt like just Rafe not being arrested for murder, that’s his win. He’s not in jail for the rest of his life. DEADLINE: Still, it feels sad for him not being able to walk his sister down the aisle. BURKE : The intent was, it felt like as good as you could possibly get for someone who was so bad for a lot of the series. It was as realistic as you can get with him being as bad as he had been, and so we wanted to thread the needle where he had to pay to some extent. He’s exiled, but he does get a second chance. Death Does Not Become Pogues DEADLINE: After JJ’s death in the Season 4 finale, did you consider killing off another Pogue in Season 5? You flirted with Kiara, who came very close to dying twice . JONAS PATE : Josh, we never thought of killing anybody else, do you remember? JOSH PATE : I never recall any. I didn’t want to kill anybody, I don’t want anyone else to die. JONAS PATE : I didn’t think so either. I was just trying to think, like, ‘Did we ever think about it?’ I don’t think so either. Though I would say that something’s thought about at all times. Like, you always consider, everything’s thought of at some point. Madison Bailey as Kiara in ‘Outer Banks’ Sesaon 5 Jackson Lee Davis/Netflix OGs-Only Treasure Hunt DEADLINE: In Season 5, Cleo was sidelined in the Bahamas twice. For the trip to Azerbaijan, Rafe also had a reason to stay, so the Pogues went after the Blue Crown in their original formation (sans JJ). it felt like a throwback to Season 1 and one last adventure for the OGs. Was it intentional? JOSH PATE : Yeah, I think we’re trying to chime some old vibes, classic OBX vibes on some of this season. BURKE : And also it gave Cleo a real singular moment where she did something at the end of eight on the runway, and it also set up finishing the Pope and Cleo story. But yeah, it felt good to have just the OG Pogues on one adventure. Jonas, what do you think about that? JONAS PATE : Yeah, I liked it. I mean, the whole show, honestly, was such a blessing to shoot. The process of making it was so much fun for all of us that I think that we wanted to make sure we experienced all those types of things that we had felt over the course of the season. So it was a little bit of adventure, a little bit of stuff in their home on their home turf. We tried to, as Josh said, chime all the old school, the old versions that we had done in the final season, just to make fans feel satisfied. L-R: Chase Stokes as John B, Madelyn Cline as Sarah Cameron in ‘Outer Banks’ Season 5 Jackson Lee Davis/Netflix Twinkie Lives On DEADLINE: You mentioned Cleo’s heroics, which included blowing up John B’s beloved VW van Twinkie. It made a return , first in the form of Sarah and John B’s wedding cake, and then as their Just Married van. Was this the refurbished original one or a new incarnation of Twinkie? JONAS PATE : Nellie, you really watched this, I appreciate that. It was a new incarnation of Twinkie, which is not easy to find. Over the course of the season, I think there were seven, because they kept breaking down. We had to keep replacing them. Outer Banks or Outer Realm DEADLINE: Blue Crown’s supposed powers. Why did you decide to introduce the element of immortality and did you consider at any point taking a supernatural route and bringing JJ or somebody else back to life? JOSH PATE : Actually, there’s a similar supernatural element in earlier seasons with [Carla] Limbrey. We always knew that the show was not a supernatural show but some people believe supernatural things in the world, and these kids could believe in these myths without us actually crossing the line into actual magic, which we never wanted to do. JONAS PATE : But we felt like, to your point, Josh, it’s human to be superstitious, right? I mean, that’s what a lot of religion is. So we never thought about crossing the line, but we knew that we could have characters that could believe in those types of things, and it could motivate their actions. BURKE : And we wanted to walk right up to the edge of that line, to the point of where some people believed that it was supernatural, and some people didn’t. We wanted to get right up to the edge of that line, but then not cross it. DEADLINE: So the ball of light, was it just a natural phenomenon? Because it wasn’t just Kiara; Finch, Groff and others also believed in the crown’s powers. BURKE : I would say in the staff or the people who are on this phone call that some people here thought it was supernatural, and some people thought it wasn’t. Would you say that’s true, guys? Because I said not supernatural, and I think Jonas said it wasn’t, and Josh, I don’t know what you say. JOSH PATE : I don’t think it was. I mean, it was a meteor shower. But again, two people can see the same thing, like a lightning bolt, and one can take it in a supernatural, spiritual way, as a sign or a message, and someone else can just be like, “Oh, it’s a lightning bolt.” People can interpret those two things differently. So, I think there are characters in the show that are on both sides of that fence, and all you have to do is show. It is coincidental? Well, they knew that there was a meteor shower. There was an incredible video that was captured online of this blue light during a meteor shower that basically was the template for the way we did that. That was real, so we didn’t push it that much if you’ve actually seen this one video of this girl underneath a meteor shower. Chase Stokes as John B, Rudy Pankow as JJ in ‘Outer Banks Jackson Lee Davis/Netflix © 2024 JJ’s Presence DEADLINE: So there was no consideration of bringing back JJ at any point, right? BURKE : Not in any corporeal, like not as a real person, but maybe in a dream sequence, sort of as it was. DEADLINE: But even in the flashbacks, you had younger actors portraying JJ and Kiara’s early years. Was there a conversation with Rudy to come back? JOSH PATE : Honestly, not really. We always knew we wanted to show when they first met. I don’t know, maybe glancingly, but it never got very serious. DEADLINE: In another natural-adjacent phenomenon, Kiara found herself in the eye of a hurricane when she fell overboard, which likely saved her life. It was a beautiful moment but was this supposed to be just symbolic or do we think JJ helped? BURKE : It’s what you think. Like Josh said, it’s walking right up the line, and you can think one thing or the other. Probably everyone is going to look at that and have a different interpretation. Did he really help or was it just that the eye of a storm passed over? DEADLINE: Do you have the answer? JONAS PATE : I guess I know what I think, but that’s not… . JOSH PATE : I think I know what Kara thinks. DEADLINE: What does she think? JOSH PATE : She thinks JJ helped her. Legalizing the Gold DEADLINE: I am a little confused how Rose couldn’t legalize the Royal Merchant gold for so long, and our guys did it in no time, becoming very rich. JOSH PATE : Shan, you want to take that one? Nellie, you’re just grinding us here. BURNE : We’d have to look that up. In maritime law, if you find it on land, there’s different laws. They were saying that before it was found in someone’s house, they didn’t own that house. The gold goes to the person who is from the house, but now that’s a treasure that they found underwater. That’s a maritime treasure, and I think it goes to them. But I’d have to check that to make sure. It’s a good question. But until proven otherwise, it’s because they found it in water, not on land. DEADLINE: Well, they didn’t have witnesses, so I don’t think anybody knows where they found it. And the gold was on land before getting on that boat but OK, I’m not going to go down that rabbit hole. JONAS PATE : In the scene between Rafe and Rose, she says that Ward hadn’t bought the Crain House yet, and they would backdate the sale that so when he found it, that’s his, that it came with the property. Rose Gold DEADLINE: Speaking of Rose, the Pogues rightfully scoffed when she asked them to bring her back some gold for a cut. But then we saw her at the wedding, and she kissed John B. So are they on good terms? Did she get any money out of the gold? JOSH PATE : I love these questions. I don’t think so. What do you think, Shan? BURKE : I don’t think so. I think she has hooked up with another rich guy on Outer Banks, and she’s okay. We wanted to be gracious with everybody. Like, they had some contentious relationships but they still grew up with her, she’s part of Sarah’s family, and it’s a happy ending. Everyone’s more or less on good terms. But yeah, I don’t think she got the gold. Outer Banks. Tony Crane as Groff in ‘Outer Banks’ Season 5 Jackson Lee Davis/Netflix “Seductive Charmer” DEADLINE: Rose seemed like a good, reasonable parental figure until she hooked up with Groff. Who in their right mind would associate themselves with somebody like him? JOSH PATE : I think old Tony is a seductive charmer. JONAS PATE : I mean, If you see watch the whole show, you see all the bad sides of him. JOSH PATE : Shannon and I are, we always described the character of Groff as “tennis handsome.” DEADLINE: Groff is one of the most irredeemable characters I’ve ever seen on TV. Did you try to humanize him, or was he just there for us to hate him? JONAS PATE : We like the good villain, right? JOSH PATE : We toyed with it, and there were elements that we wanted to soften. I think he’s just got a deep psychopathology that’s going on. There was this book called Blood Will Out that our buddy Walter Kirn wrote. It’s about this sociopathic guy who imitates a Rockefeller, he murders somebody, and Walter, who’d befriended him, goes to see him in prison after he’s been convicted of murder. And he’s like, “Okay, man, you lied to me about everything, and you f*cking killed somebody. And the guy looks right at Walter and goes like, “I didn’t kill him.” He’s still lying. That’s what we just kept thinking about. Like, wow, this guy can really go all the way. BURKE : There’s that moment where he has the painting of Larissa, he’s talking to Larissa. I don’t think he’s redeemed, but I think it’s explicable that his original sin is that he married up into Larissa’s family, and then he ends up killing her, and then he’s trying to go back to reverse this thing that he did initially. He’s obviously insane, he’s gone crazy, so not redeemed in any way, but maybe explicable? From left: Austin North as Topper (golfing), Drew Starkey as Rafe, Jason Davis as Dale, Mia Challis as Ruthie in ‘Outer Banks’ Season 5 Jackson Lee Davis/Netflix The Case Of The Disappearing Kooks DEADLINE: Can you explain how the Kooks disappeared somehow, and how in the world is Topper now a bartender? Don’t the Kooks have wealth? BURKE : Well, even wealthy people – they still work as bartenders, they have trouble. The intent was to soften him, to make him more relatable, like he’s actually learned something. JOSH PATE : I think he’s been excommunicated from his parents a little bit too. He’s had a lot of trouble with his mom and dad, so maybe he got cut off and has to support himself now as a bartender. But again, yeah, to make him a little bit more likable, as Shannon would say. DEADLINE: But Kooks still live there, they are just not as rich as they were? There seems to be a clear shift in the dynamic on the island . JOSH PATE : I think the Kooks abandoned the island after the hurricane to a large extent because the island’s destroyed, and what’s happened in the coastal Carolinas is, you can’t get insurance anymore. So they’ll pay you back, but they won’t let you rebuild, and that’s kind of it. Kind of like what’s happening in LA, and so I think, the post-hurricane island returns to more a poorer version of the island. Acknowledgments DEADLINE: Any final thoughts about your Outer Banks journey and ending the show on your own terms? JOSH PATE : We feel really a lot of gratitude to being allowed to end the show in the way we wanted to. A lot of gratitude to Netflix, to Ted [Sarandos] and Bela [Bajaria] and Nne [Ebong], who believed in the show from the beginning, and they largely let us tell the story that we wanted to. So, you’ve been around Hollywood long enough to know that you rarely get to end on your own terms. So, we feel a lot of gratitude for that. Camila Morrone Stars In ‘Miami Vice ’85’ With Michael B. title: Jaafar Jackson Says ‘Michael’ Sequel “Will Give Even More Insight” Into Child Abuse Allegations “From His Point Of View”

In a new interview, Jaafar Jackson said he would want his uncle’s point of view on all the child abuse allegations. “I think the second film will give even more insight from his point of view, because at the end of the day, [the allegations] are always from someone else’s,” Jaafar Jackson said in an interview with GQ Middle East . title: Dave Bautista Officially Cast as Kratos in ‘God of War’ Series
full_text: Skip to main content By Rick Porter Plus Icon Rick Porter Television Business Editor rickporter Follow Sign Up View All August 20, 2026 3:19pm Dave Bautista Mike Coppola/Getty Images Logo text Prime Video ‘s God of War series has found a new lead actor to replace the injured Ryan Hurst. Dave Bautista will on the role of Kratos in the series, which is based on the long-running video game franchise. Hurst ( The Odyssey, Sons of Anarchy ) was originally cast in the role but had to step aside after tearing a bicep while performing a stunt on set. Prime Video confirmed Bautista’s casting after initial reports in early August that the actor was in talks to take over the role. Related Stories TV 'Sterling Point' Renewed for Season 2 at Prime Video TV Chris Pratt Returns to Battle for Redemption in 'Terminal List' Season 2 Trailer Bautista is a known quantity to both viewers — via Marvel’s Guardians of the Galaxy films, Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery and Dune Part Two , plus his time as a WWE star — and Amazon MGM Studios, which is producing God of War with Sony Pictures Television. Bautista has appeared in Amazon MGM’s two My Spy movies and The Wrecking Crew and has roles in the studio’s forthcoming features Highlander and Road House 2 . With Bautista now officially on board, the goal is to get God of War back into production in Vancouver in the fall. The show’s cast also includes Callum Vinson , Mandy Patinkin , Ed Skrein , Max Parker, Ólafur Darri Ólafsson, Teresa Palmer, Alastair Duncan, Jeff Gulka and Danny Woodburn. The series will follow Kratos and his son, Atreus, as they “embark on a journey to spread the ashes of their wife and mother, Faye,” per the show’s logline. “Through their adventures, Kratos tries to teach his son to be a better god, while Atreus tries to teach his father how to be a better human.” The series will be based primarily on the two most recent installments of the game franchise, which introduced Atreus. Ronald D. Moore ( For All Mankind, Outlander ), who has an overall deal at Sony, is the showrunner and executive produces with Maril Davis, Cory Barlog, Naren Shankar, Matthew Graham, Asad Qizilbash, Jeff Ketcham, Hermen Hulst, Roy Lee, and Brad Van Arragon. Joe Menosky, Marc Bernardin, Tania Lotia, and Ben McGinnis are co-EPs. Frederick E.O. Toye is set to direct the first two episodes. Sony and Amazon MGM are producing God of War with PlayStation Productions and Moore’s Tall Ship Productions. Bautista is repped by WME and Jackoway Austen. Aug. 20, 3:18 p.m. Updated throughout with confirmation of Bautista’s casting. This story was initially published on Aug. 3, 2026. THR

title: ‘Insidious: Out Of The Further’ To Scare Up $50M+ WW; ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ To Prevail With $85M+ WW In Fourth Frame – Box Office Preview
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News California Film & TV Tax Credits In Peril As Sacramento Deal Falls Apart: Exclusive Read the full story By Anthony D'Alessandro Anthony D'Alessandro Editorial Director/Box Office Editor @AwardsTony More Stories By Anthony ‘Insidious: Out Of The Further’ To Scare Up $50M+ WW; ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ To Prevail With $85M+ WW In Fourth Frame – Box Office Preview The ParaBros Backlash: Threats To Leave L.A. & An AG Who Won’t Back Down Divide Hollywood A24’s Kate Fassl Joins Ari Aster’s Square Peg As Head Of Comms & Talent Relations View All August 20, 2026 3:15pm 'Insidious Out of the Further' and 'Spider-Man Brand New Day' Sony Dog days of August? What dog days of August do you speak of? Absolutely none here as Spider-Man: Brand New Day heads for a healthy fourth weekend of $35 million at this weekend’s domestic box office, and $85M worldwide. That 50% fourth-weekend decline is on par with Disney/Marvel’s Avengers: Endgame. Related Stories News ‘Insidious: Out Of The Further’ Review: Horror Franchise Returns With A New Family & PG-13 Zombie Twist That Feels A Bit Stale News The 65 Movies That Have Made More Than $1 Billion At The Global Box Office As we told you, Spider-Man ‘s fourth weekend in North America will likely not be one for the record books; the best fourth weekend at the domestic B.O. belongs to Warner Bros’ American Sniper at $89.3M, followed by Avatar with $50.3M. How high will Sony’s highest-grossing movie ever with $2 billion-plus go? It likely won’t topple the high points of 20th Century Studio’s Avatar ($2.9B) or Avengers: Endgame ($2.79B, and will raise its grosses more after its September re-issue). However, Brand New Day has a shot at pushing China’s animated Ne Zha 2 further down on the charts (that pic grossed $2.27B). Watch on Deadline As we told you earlier this week, Spider-Man: Brand New Day became the fastest film to cross $800M in 19 days stateside. The movie remains in competition with history; Disney/Lucasfilm’s Star Wars: The Forc e Awakens is the only movie ever to cross $900M in North America. Sony will likely have bragging rights for No. 2 stateside this upcoming frame with Blumhouse Atomic Monster’s $18M spinoff Insidious: Out of the Further , which is looking at $23M-$27M at 3,303 theaters. The previous installment, 2023’s Insidious: The Red Door, came in well ahead of expectations for the 16-year-old PG-13 spooky franchise with a $33M start (though not a record; that’s still owned by Insidious 2 at $40.2M), knocking out Indiana Jones and the Dial of Destiny in its second weekend. Red Door is considered a bit of a unicorn as it was a reunion of the franchise’s original cast Rose Byrne and Patrick Wilson, the latter making his feature directorial debut. The pic wound up becoming the highest-grossing in the franchise with $189M worldwide. The entire Insidious franchise’s global gross to date is nearly $732M. Insidious: Out of the Further will share PLFs with Spider-Man: Brand New Day . Imax will be split between Brand New Day and Odyssey. Previews start in U.S.-Canada at 2 p.m.. Rotten Tomatoes critics are at 60% fresh for Out of the Further. Overseas, Insidious: Out of the Further, which stars franchise’s thespian Lin Shaye and is directed and written by Come Play ‘s Jacob Chase, is looking at $26M in 64 territories for a global start between $49M-$53M . The offshore forecast of $26M is around where Insidious 3 and Insidious: The Last Key were. These supernatural movies do well in Catholic countries, and already we’re hearing that Out of the Further has posted the best opening day for a horror movie ever in the Philippines ( Red Door opened to $3.7M there). Shaye traveled to Peru, so expect at pop at the B.O. there ( Red Door opened to a reported $1M there). The sequel won’t be going in Japan or China, but will be scaring up Korea in addition to other major foreign territories. Overall, Out of the Further will be another test for franchise horror in a year dominated by YouTube genre creators via Obsession and Backrooms. Scream 7 is by far the biggest horror franchise opener YTD with $97.2M WW (and $63.6M domestic). Those numbers were also record starts in the series for that Kevin Williamson franchise. ‘ Spa Weekend ‘ Black Bear Others wides entries at the domestic B.O. this weekend are in the single-digits range, i.e., Black Bear’s Spa Weekend from The Hangover architects Jon Lucas and Scott Moore, at 2,009 sites with $3M-$5M. Pic stars Anna Faris, Isla Fisher, Michelle Buteau and Leslie Mann and follows a group of friends (and the one GF they box out) at a posh spa resort where they wreck havoc. Lionsgate has the Jean-François Richet-directed Jason Statham movie Mutiny , which follows a guy aboard a cargo ship on a one-man crusade after witnessing his billionaire boss’ murder and is framed for the crime. Statham’s protag is out to avenge his boss’ death only to discover an international conspiracy. The studio has released a long list of Statham movies. The R-rated pic’s previews start at 5 p.m. today. Critics are 49% Rotten on Statham’s latest. Mutiny is booked at 2,703 theaters in U.S./Canada.

title: Dave Bautista Set To Play Kratos In ‘God Of War’ As Amazon Series Recasts Lead
full_text: Skip to main content By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie Trouble In Paradise: John Ross Bowie & Brian Posehn On Who Ruined Utopia In ‘Stuart Fails’ E5 ‘Outer Banks’ Creators Break Down Season 5’s “Earned” Ending, Supernatural Lean & JJ’s Presence Dave Bautista Set To Play Kratos In ‘God Of War’ As Amazon Series Recasts Lead View All August 20, 2026 3:00pm Dave Bautista; Kratos from 'God of War' Getty Imagesx Dave Bautista has closed his deal to play Kratos in Prime Video’s God of War fantasy drama series. Series co-studios Amazon MGM Studios and Sony Pictures Television reached out to Bautista and initiated talks shortly after they made the decision to recast the role following original lead Ryan Hurst’s serious on-set injury. As Deadline reported , Hurst, who had been originally cast as Kratos in the adaptation of the popular PlayStation video game, tore a bicep while performing a stunt in late June, four months into the shoot. Related Stories News Film Buyers Fume As Amazon Accidentally Leaks Jason Statham's Big-Budget 'Mutiny' Ahead Of Cinema Release: "A Multimillion-Dollar Problem" News English Football Giants Liverpool Confirm Sale Of Stake To Jeff Bezos & Facebook Co-Founder Eduardo Saverin Bautista’s casting signals a possible different approach to the character of Kratos, which has been the subject of intense online discourse following the first-look image released in February . Watch on Deadline Prep begins this month for a mid-October production start in Vancouver where the show is based. The series is starting from scratch as no footage from the original shoot is being used. Emmy-winning director Frederick E.O. Toye ( Shōgun, The Boys, Fallout ), who directed the first two episodes with Hurst, will do the same for the new iteration with Bautista. The fall production start leaves little time for Bautista to get ready to play the physically demanding role of Kratos but his extensive background as a professional wrestler is expected to kick in, along with the work he had done recently for his role in the new Highlander movie , which required him to bulk up. The ancient mythology-themed God of War, from writer, executive producer and showrunner Ronald D. Moore, began filming in February in Vancouver on a two-season order with the seasons slated to film back-to-back, which remains the plan. God of War follows father and son Kratos (Bautista) and Atreus (Callum Vinson) as they embark on a journey to spread the ashes of their wife and mother, Faye. Through their adventures, Kratos tries to teach his son to be a better god, while Atreus tries to teach his father how to be a better human. The titular character of the entire franchise, Kratos is Spartan by birth, and a god by nature. Giles Keyte/Amazon MGM Studios Logo text After an underwhelming box-office take in movie theaters, Masters of the Universe found a softer landing in its streaming debut. The movie based on the 1980s cartoon series and toys scored the No. 1 overall ranking in Nielsen’s streaming ratings for July 20-26, its first week of streaming. The top two original titles for the week were Will Ferrell’s Netflix comedy The Hawk (944 million minutes) and Prime Video’s action comedy Ride or Die (922 million), starring Octavia Spencer and Hannah Waddingham. The Hawk declined slightly week to week, while Ride or Die ticked up by about 6 percent. The debut of King of the Hill ‘ s 15th season pushed the animated series back onto the charts with 658 million minutes of watch time, 70 percent of which (about 461 million minutes) came from the new batch of episodes. Netflix’s Ransom Canyon (751 million minutes) also returned to the rankings with the premiere of its second season. Netflix’s Kevin Hart comedy 72 Hours placed second behind Masters of the Universe on the movies top 10 with a solid 791 million minutes for its premiere week. full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News California Film & TV Tax Credits In Peril As Sacramento Deal Falls Apart: Exclusive Read the full story By Jill Goldsmith Jill Goldsmith Co-Business Editor More Stories By Jill The ParaBros Backlash: Threats To Leave L.A. & An AG Who Won’t Back Down Divide Hollywood Peacock Hikes Prices Across All Subscription Plans Cinema United Urges Paramount’s David Ellison, California AG To Resolve Differences; Cinemark Throws Support Behind Merger View All August 11, 2026 7:31am Story Arc The Paramount lot in Los Angeles Getty Images Paramount CEO David Ellison told a group of the company’s top executives that he will start the process of exiting California on October 1 if the state’s Attorney General Rob Bonta will not negotiate to settle an antitrust suit around the planned merger with Warner Bros. Discovery. Bonta has just responded: “In a span of weeks, Paramount agreed to halt the merger until a court decision or until June 2027, asked for a November trial, and is now back with another attempt to blackmail the state into letting an illegal deal through. Paramount has lost the plot as it continues to lose in court. It didn’t work the first time — on the eve of our July lawsuit — and it won’t work this time.” Ellison made the remarks at a meeting last week. Details were first reported by Puck and confirmed by Deadline. Watch on Deadline Related Stories Commentary Don’t Believe Paramount’s Hype: California AG Rob Bonta Claims David Ellison Muddying WBD Merger Waters With Misinformation & Side Deals; “We Intend To Win” – Guest Column News Paramount Making Deals To Theaters For 30 Films A Year Post-WBD Acquisition; Cinema United Still Anti-Merger Bonta is leading a group of 20 state Attorneys General in the case that is set to go to trial in federal court in the Northern District of California March 2027. October 1 is the day Paramount starts to accrue a so-called ticking fee of $7 million a day agreed to in the WBD deal terms if the transaction hasn’t closed by then. Paramount had asked the judge for a November trial date. Deadline hears that Ellison was emphatic at the meeting that he does not want to relocate but also doesn’t feel welcome in Paramount’s home state as the company and the AG wage a PR battle. The $111 billion merger has been approved by the DOJ and international regulatory agencies, including in the EU and UK. The AGs’ suit is focused on antitrust claims in three areas: wide release films, blockbuster films and cable network programming. Ellison has promised the combined studios will release 30 films a year with significant theatrical windows. He has said he offered to put that in writing for the AG and otherwise engage in settlement talks around potential concessions. A relocation would start with the company’s headquarters, followed by studio jobs. Ellison would move Paramount, or the merged Paramount-WBD , regardless of the outcome of a trial. Beyond the ticking fee, Paramount would owe WBD a $7 billion termination fee (the largest in corporate history) if the deal falls apart unless Warner’s board, led by CEO David Zaslav, agrees to renegotiate. WBD can walk if the deal is not clinched by June 4. Rumors had surfaced months ago that Ellison was considering a California exit if the AG did not soften his stance. Destinations mentioned have included Tennessee, Texas and Georgia. Potential new home states have presumably offered significant incentives if Paramount relocates. In response to previous threats to leave the state, Bonta has called it a “last ditch effort to try to blackmail my office and the attorneys general into allowing an illegal deal.” Paramount has accused Bonta of playing politics. In an op-ed published in Deadline on Monday, the California AG said “Paramount and Warner Bros see the writing on the wall: that they will lose in a court of law. So instead, they are resorting to the court of public opinion. They want to talk about anything but the facts of this case… As disingenuous as it may be, they are welcome to do so.” The California Film Commission on Monday announced that Paramount’s Alicia Silverstone -starring Clueless series and EGOT superstar Viola Davis ‘ corporate fixer series Ascent have been allocated nearly $38 million in Golden State tax incentives under its sweetened package to curb runaway production. In a note this morning, Richard Greenfield at Lightshed Partners wrote that “everything Paramount has done over the past several weeks appears to be inflaming the situation with California Attorney General Rob Bonta and increasing the odds this case goes to trial in March 2027. Given that the merger agreement expires on June 4, 2027, going to trial is a suicide mission that will likely lead to the merger collapsing and the Ellison family being forced to pay the $7 billion breakup fee.” Noting favorable deal commentary by Ari Emanuel, AMC Entertainment CEO Adam Aron and Regal chief Eduardo Acuna, Greenfield said, “Ellison has effectively rallied every major Hollywood ally he can find. What he has not done is offer any form of structural remedy that Bonta and the other State AGs might be willing to accept.” Rather, “Paramount’s PR campaign appears to be strengthening Bonta’s hand rather than weakening it. Bonta was already operating from a position of strength: the judge granted the temporary restraining order and appeared favorably disposed to the State AGs’ antitrust claims, set a March 2027 trial date despite Paramount’s hopes for a November 2026 trial and has shown no inclination to move at Paramount’s preferred pace given the ticking fee and the June 4 merger termination date.” The ope-ed in Deadline, Greenfield said, “makes it crystal clear that Paramount’s approach is making things worse and that the State AGs have no intention of settling this case.” Camila Morrone Stars In ‘Miami Vice ’85’ With Michael B. AMC Entertainment and Regal, the top two circuits, have supported David Ellison’s bid to buy WBD, a process that’s slowed considerably due to an antitrust lawsuit by a dozen state attorneys general. Bonta is leading the charge to block the deal. A trial is set for March. Yesterday, Paramount’s lawyers filed paperwork seeking a $1.88 billion bond from blue state AG plaintiffs and the WGA. That bond would help cover the $7 million-a-day ticking fee that Paramount Skydance is obliged to pay to WBD shareholders starting in a few weeks, plus other costs baked into the agreement. Cinema United’s note: Dear Attorney General Bonta and Mr. Ellison, We are writing to you in our capacity as the leadership of Cinema United, the world’s largest trade organization representing the global theatrical exhibition business. We write to encourage you both to meet in the immediate future and discuss all possible avenues for resolving the state of California’s pending challenge to Paramount’s proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. Theatrical exhibition is a Main Street industry. A night at the cinema not only benefits the movie studios and theatre owners, but it also benefits nearby restaurants, coffee shops, bars and shopping frequented by moviegoers. From family-owned independent theatres to vibrant mid-size circuits to the world’s largest theatre chains, Cinema United members are cultural and economic drivers in communities across this great nation. Our members have been partnering with Paramount and Warner Bros. for over a century to provide movie fans of all ages with the unparalleled experience of a movie on the big screen. We look forward to strengthening and growing that proud tradition for generations to come. Movie theatres are also undeniably a part of the fabric of this nation. In just the twelve states represented in the litigation we have 196 members doing business. The majority of those are independent or family-owned theatres: 130 operate fewer than ten screens; 90, with less than five screens; and 30 of those members operate single-screen theaters. Our industry is familiar with the impact of legacy studio consolidation on moviegoers and exhibition, and those facts are well documented. As a result, all relevant parties understand the enduring value of the theatrical experience not only to our culture, but to the overall economy and the financial success of films themselves. At the same time, we have remained open to tangible and enforceable guardrails that can offer our industry some measure of certainty in the face of an evolving and otherwise challenging future. That is why we have engaged, in good faith, with both the coalition of State Attorneys General and Paramount. As you both know, we believe any resolution of the current situation must ensure four core elements, which are essential to the long-term strength of the entertainment industry: A long-term commitment to maintain or expand wide-release theatrical movie production that is supported by a meaningful period of theatrical exclusivity, fully marketed, and promoted in theatres of all sizes. Provisions ensuring that the merger will not cause an increase in rental terms, so that theatre owners, and in turn, moviegoers, do not bear the brunt of the cost of this transaction, particularly independent theatres across the United States. Enforceable safeguards to ensure broad access to films for moviegoers and theatres of all sizes that is not conditioned on requirements that impede theatre owners from making business decisions that are responsive to their communities’ preferences and the broader marketplace realities that many theatre owners face today. And finally, continued access, under reasonable conditions and precedents, to the valuable and vast film catalogues of both Paramount and Warner Bros. Today, our industry has the wind at its back. Studio partners are creating and distributing extraordinary films. Audiences across generations are responding with enthusiasm. Theatre owners are continuing to reinvest in their cinemas and build remarkable experiences for moviegoers. Movies are once again at the center of our shared culture. But none of that can be taken for granted. Global exhibition believes in a bold future for this industry, but reaching our full potential requires working together. For many in our industry, the current environment is marked by disruption and uncertainty. That is why we believe that it is incumbent upon both of you to meet in good faith to discuss a resolution that would provide robust protections and serve the entire industry. In fact, it is the next logical step. Our goal remains a resolution that puts this industry on a positive path to continued success, not just in the near-term, but for generations to come. As has been the case since the outset, we stand ready to assist in any way we can. However, we urge you both to take the steps necessary to explore a meaningful resolution of the current situation as soon as possible. Camila Morrone Stars In ‘Miami Vice ’85’ With Michael B. title: Decision On Paramount’s $1.88B WBD Merger Bond Pushed Close To Ticking Fee Start Date; L.A. County…
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News California Film & TV Tax Credits In Peril As Sacramento Deal Falls Apart: Exclusive Read the full story By Dominic Patten Dominic Patten Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics @DeadlineDominic More Stories By Dominic Decision On Paramount’s $1.88B WBD Merger Bond Pushed Close To Ticking Fee Start Date; L.A. County Report Again Predicts Big Job Losses If Deal Goes Through Technical Foul: Buss Family Dispute Now Leaves Lakers Stake Sale To Bob Iger & Josh Kushner In Purgatory Put Up Or Shut Up! Paramount Demands A Huge Bond From AGs & WGA Over Costs Of “Roadblock” Antitrust Suit On WBD Merger View All August 19, 2026 2:05pm Story Arc Paramount and Warner Bros. lot Getty The results of a court hearing in Oakland on Wednesday might be a little to close for comfort for Paramount and David Ellison . Additionally, the findings of a report submitted to the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors might prove very scary in terms of potential job losses and more if the $111 billion merger with Warner Bros Discovery goes through. Related Stories News Parties Lay Out Key Discovery And Other Dates For Pending Paramount-WBD Antitrust Trial Executives Paramount’s Precipice: How David Ellison Could Salvage $111B WBD Merger (Hint – Call Kamala) As fellow billionaire Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta faces 29 states down the street in California court over potentially trillions in penalties and allegations that his social media platforms violated child privacy laws and are constructed to be addictive, lawyers for CEO Ellison were in federal court Monday hoping to get their recent $1.88 billion bond request addressed ASAP. With a trial in the 12-state antitrust case against the melding Paramount and Warner Bros Discovery already set for March 2027, it all turned out to be a session of hurry up and wait. Watch on Deadline Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin decided this morning that nothing is going to happen in that big flex by Paramount until September 24. That’s just days before the $7 million a day ticking fee to WBD shareholders kicks in on October 1. A stipulation of the agreement from earlier this year between Team Ellison and the David Zaslav-run WBD that could rack up close to $1.3 billion in payouts (if the deal goes south or is pushed back) for the still Melrose lot based company. Fees that, along with some regulatory hoops Paramount will have to rejump through in February, that make up a significant portion of Para’s request August 17 motion for the big money to offset the “extraordinary losses” the state’s July 13 filed case could cause the company. There’s also a June 4 deadline for the expiration of a deal, with Paramount obliged to pay a $7 billion termination fee. Not cheap, even for the scion of one time world’s richest man Larry Ellison (who has committed some very big bucks to guaranteing the debt heavy WBD deal). The Oracle founder was nowhere to be seen or heard today, but plaintiffs’ lead attorney California’s Ashley Kaplan, plus fellow lawyers James Weingarten, Bren Nakamura, Richard Parker, Kellie Lerner, Julia May, Nicole Gordon, Divya Rao, Joseph Alioto, and Christina Black were onboard virtually for CA AG Rob Bonta , NY AG Letitia James, 10 other blue states and the Writers Guild of America in the hearing. Beth Wilkinson (maybe the busiest lawyer in Tinseltown this summer), Rakesh Kilaru, Jeffrey Kessler, Marguerite Sullivan, Dan Petrocelli, Pete Herrick, Julia Schiller, Maggie Sullivan and Jennifer Parsigian were there for Paramount and WBD. The bond may be a long overdue grown up move by Paramount in the bitter battle in court and the court of public opinion. However, it could also ultimately prove an empty gesture too. In a TRO ruling last month, the Joe Biden-appointed judge cast aside the need for a bond, $1.88 billion or otherwise. “Plaintiffs have demonstrated that Plaintiff States bring suit to enforce important public interests,” Martinez-Olguin said in a pretty heavily implied rejection of the security requirement. Still, courts like casinos are full of wild card moments, so that could all shift by late September, or not. The Ronald V. Dellums Federal Building complex in downtown Oakland, CA Jane Tyska/Digital First Media/East Bay Times via Getty Images With all that playing out in Northern California, the L.A. County Department of Economic Opportunity to today built on its already ominous June 18 report to the board of supervisors on a Para-WBD merger with even harsher data. If the $82 billion debt carrying ParaBros was to be real, David Ellison’s dream will be a nightmare for Paramount and WBD staff, the “Assessing the Effects of the Proposed Paramount Skydance Acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery on the Los Angeles County Economy and Workforce” entitled dense document predicts. There will be “a potential loss of 15,567 corporate roles that overlap across both companies, with 6,099 shared, and 2,495 jobs specifically in Los Angeles County,” today’s report says. Read the L.A. County Department of Economic Opportunity report on possible consequences of a Paramount-WBD merger here. Getting very specific in the realm of some of the worst fears of both critics and boasters of the merger, the DEO document goes on to cite: • If the merger goes through, about 4,500 film and TV jobs in Los Angeles County could be lost over the three-year period when the companies combine operations • In total, 10,360 job years could be at risk, including: — 2,661 indirect jobs at small businesses that support production — such as prop houses, printers, transportation companies, and other vendors. — 3,204 induced jobs that exist because film and TV workers spend money in the local economy including restaurants, retailers, and service providers. • The economic impact of losing these jobs is significant. At stake: — $1.26 billion in wages — $2.78 billion in economic value — $4.06 billion in total business output — $547 million in tax revenue, including $78.6 million in local taxes — most of which (63%) comes from property taxes. With initial details from two months ago in mind, the report notes: These estimates measure employment capacity at risk, not a forecast of layoffs. One job sustained for one year equals one job-year, so the impact may be distributed across different workers, projects, and positions over the three-year integration period. • The impact extends beyond direct film and television employment. An estimated 2,661 indirect job-years are at risk among businesses that support production, including independent artists, agents and promoters, sound recording, employment services, and equipment rental. A further 3,204 induced job-years reflect reduced household spending across the County economy. • The economic impact extends well beyond employment. The modeled losses correspond to approximately $1.26 billion in labor income, $2.79 billion in value added, and $4.06 billion in economic output over the modeled period. • The fiscal impact extends across federal, state, and local government. The modeled losses correspond to approximately $547 million in tax revenue, including $78.6 million in local tax revenue. • Impacts would emerge over time, not at closing. Evidence from six completed media mergers shows workforce actions unfolding over several years following a transaction, supporting continued monitoring of employment and production activity rather than a single point-in-time assessment. To put this into perspective, the direct jobs at risk account for nearly 9% of the 52,016 film and TV jobs California has already lost since 2022 — and almost all those losses (99.6%) occurred in Los Angeles County. Do the math, all of it. Paramount had their own POV on the DEO report. “ LA County ’s own economic report underscores what we have been saying all along: our industry is in decline, production is down and jobs are being lost — and lost for good if we don’t act,” a company spokesperson told Deadline Wednesday. “Our plan to invest $30 billion annually in production and release at least 30 films a year is how we regain that ground: more production that supports more jobs over time, and ultimately, a stronger, more durable entertainment industry for generations to come.” In a posting on X, Bonta said of the latest L.A. County report: “As I have said repeatedly, the proposed unlawful Paramount-Warner Brothers merger will lead to significant job loss and massive damage to the economy.” Meanwhile, back in Oakland, as various exhibitors, guilds and pundits opine on the pros and cons of one big ParaBros, and Team Ellison leaks threats to adiós California and jump to a friendlier Red jurisdiction, today’s 21-minute case management conference before Martinez-Olguin had some other topics on the agenda too. For one thing, all sides said in an August 13 filing they “are having constructive discussions regarding the identification of two alternative magistrate judges to preside over a settlement conference for the Actions and will provide a further update to the Court as soon as possible.” Now, this is standard operating procedure in matters such as this, and leans not much at all to the desires of the DGA, the suddenly corporately compliant IATSE and others for a deal to avoid a trial. To that, Magistrate Judge Ajay Krishnan, who took on his role in January, has been named to oversee discovery. No judge has been picked “for mediation,” but filings (AKA suggestions) from the AGs/ WGA and Para/WBD are due on August 26. Looking forward to the May 2 – 19 trial, Judge Martinez-Olguin indicated she was going to have her courtroom open to the public – which may make this a streaming drama by any other name. Neither Paramount nor Golden State AG Bonta’s office responded to Deadline’s request for comment on today’s hearing. California Attorney General Rob Bonta left, Paramount CEO David Ellison Getty Images Paramount shares closed down a hair Wednesday at $10.60, off more than 20% year to date (despite gaining over the past few weeks) and half of where they were trading at their 52-week high of over $20. Overall, the $31-a-share cash deal is funded by mix of equity and debt. Larry Ellison is personally guaranteeing $45.7 billion in equity commitments (with much of that syndicated out to Middle East investors); the debt package of about $49 billion is run through a group of banks led by Citibank, Bank of America and Apollo. Para would assume WBD’s debt, reported at about $30 billion net as of June 30. Jill Goldsmith contributed to this report Camila Morrone Stars In ‘Miami Vice ’85’ With Michael B.
